This work deliberately belongs to the Chinese correlative and holistic tradition. It does not fall within Western science in the narrow sense — the science that proceeds by reduction, falsifiability and consensus. It belongs to \textbf{correlative science}, which proceeds by structural analogy, isomorphism and resonance.

It is therefore important to clarify from the outset the meaning of the terms employed, in order to avoid any misunderstanding:

The Western reader is invited to suspend his or her usual criteria and to enter the correlative logic, which is neither inferior nor superior to his or her own — it is different. The Eastern reader is invited to recognize an approach that belongs to his or her own tradition, that of the Yi Jing, the Wuxing and the Bagua.

\paragraph{Status of the connections established.}
The connections established in this work are of three kinds:
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{0pt}
\item \textbf{Structural connections}: $64 \to 20$ isomorphism between particle physics, the genetic code, Mandarin phonology, Tang alliances and political economy.
\item \textbf{Correlative connections}: correspondences between Chinese tradition (Wuxing, Yi Jing, Bagua) and topological structures (pentads, Merkabah, Cl(6,6)).
\item \textbf{Speculative connections}: hypotheses on the causal mechanism (why 72 emerges, why $\Lambda_{72} \subset \mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$, etc.).
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Three cross-cutting distinctions.}
Beyond the glossary, three distinctions run through the entire work and must be kept in mind. They make it possible to read each chapter without over-interpreting what it asserts.

\textbf{(1) Admissible bounds vs. exact number.} The geometry of $\mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$ \textbf{filters} the space of configurations; it does not \textbf{determine} the exact number of states that realize each configuration. The Merkabah topology sets the \textbf{admissible bounds} (the 20 attractors, the 5 phases of the Wuxing, the 4 polarity signatures) and the \textbf{differential distribution of the redundancy potential} (the $3P$ classes limit redundancy to 1--2 codons, the $1P+2N$ classes allow up to 6). Historical systems — biological, linguistic, economic — populate the coordinates \textit{within} these bounds, according to their functional and evolutionary constraints. In short: \textbf{the geometry predicts the architecture of the landscape; the system populates its coordinates}.

\textbf{(2) Encode vs. understand.} The $\mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$ formalism \textbf{encodes} structural signatures; it does not \textbf{understand} the phenomena it models. A codon does not "mean" an amino acid, it encodes it via an invariant physicochemical signature. Likewise, the spectral dashboard does not "understand" the economy; it projects it into a topological space where the structure is preserved. This orthogonality between structural encoding and semantic understanding is what makes the formalism usable as a tool of regulation: it does not claim to say what a situation \textit{means}, it says which \textit{structure} it presents.

\textbf{(3) Native interpretability vs. semantic interpretation.} The proposed architecture offers a \textbf{native interpretability}: each state corresponds to a known pentad triplet, each transition follows a deterministic geometric rule, each change of regime is traced via the spectral observables. This interpretability is \textit{native} in the sense that it is constitutive of the formalism, not added after the fact by approximate explanation techniques. It does not, however, constitute a \textbf{semantic interpretation} in the usual sense: it describes the \textbf{topological structure} of the signature, not its "meaning". This distinction is the same as the one that separates the genetic code from the meaning of proteins.

\paragraph{Project of this work.}
This work does not seek validation in the Western manner. It does not claim to prescribe to the Chinese what they should do — the implementation of the Territorial Regeneration Rent (TRR) and of the diplomacy of regeneration is already under way. It is not a matter of teaching music to those who are already playing it.

This work proposes the \textbf{mathematical apparatus} — spectral observables, topological indicators, bifurcation thresholds, arithmetic gates, multi-resolution dashboards — that makes it possible to steer the whole of the economy while integrating the geographic dimension in a holistic way.

\paragraph{The holistic integration of geography and economics.}
This is where the novelty of this work lies. Until now, economic thought has treated geography in three ways:
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{0pt}
\item \textbf{Classical economics} (Smith, Ricardo, Marx) abstracts space.
\item \textbf{Spatial economics} (von Thünen, Christaller, Lösch, Krugman) adds space as a variable.
\item \textbf{Structural geography} (Rebour) theorizes space as form.
\end{itemize}

This work proposes for the first time a \textbf{holistic integration} of geography and economics: the Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(6,0) \otimes \mathrm{Cl}(0,6)$, where economics and geography are two facets of a single topological structure.

\end{tcolorbox}

\paragraph{Topological vs. semantic status.}
Let us specify from the outset that this work does not constitute a semantic model in the sense of contemporary distributed embeddings. The Clifford algebra does not capture linguistic similarity or the "meaning" of economic phenomena — it encodes \textbf{structural signatures} preserving the $64 \to 20$ topology. This property is orthogonal to semantic similarity, exactly as the genetic code is orthogonal to the "meaning" of proteins: a codon does not "mean" an amino acid, it encodes it via an invariant physicochemical signature. The system does not "understand" the economy; it projects it into a topological space where the structure is preserved, guaranteeing a native interpretability without external supervision.

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=blue!5!white,colframe=blue!75!black,title=In one sentence]
The reader who is looking for a falsifiable theory in the Popperian sense will not find one here — and that is deliberate. The reader who is looking for a steering instrument for integrated economics-geography will find one — and that is the point.
\end{tcolorbox}

\section*{Executive summary}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Executive summary}

\textit{This summary is addressed to decision-makers. It presents the diagnosis, the solution and the strategic implications without mathematical formalism. For the theoretical foundations, see Parts II and IV.}

\subsection{The fundamental problem}

Conventional economic models (DSGE, macroeconometric forecasts) have systematically failed to anticipate the major crises: 1929, 1973, 2008, 2022. Their error is structural: they treat the economy as a continuous space of adjustable variables, whereas it functions as a \textbf{discrete information system}, with sharp rupture thresholds and stable regimes.

The structural crisis that China is going through today — collapse of the real-estate market, asphyxiating municipal debt, halt of mega-infrastructure — is neither an anomaly nor an ideological failure. It is the foreseeable halt of a growth engine that has simply exhausted its energy.

\subsection{The hidden mechanism of growth}

Contrary to classical theories, strong growth is not born of equilibrium, but of \textbf{disequilibrium}. It rests on the transfer of "dormant" assets (unexploited land) towards the real economy, financed by borrowing. This mechanism enriches a country rapidly, but it has an absolute limit: when the stock of land or infrastructure that can be easily mobilized is exhausted, the machine stops.

\textbf{The historical burden — 2,000 years of fatal cycles.} The application of this mechanism to Chinese history reveals a repetitive tragedy. For two millennia, the empire experienced nine great collapses (from the Han to the Republic). Each time the same scenario: when the elites had monopolized all the land, the peasants suffocated until violent revolt. The empire had no peaceful tool to restart its economic machine; only destruction made it possible to restart the economy.

\subsection{The Chinese dead end of 2018}

From 1978 to 2018, China reproduced this Western model on the scale of its continent, using the sale of land by municipalities (Tudi Caizheng) to finance its frenetic development. In 2018, the stock of available land dried up: the wall had been reached. Faced with this blockage, hoping that artificial intelligence, data or carbon will replace real estate is an illusion: these sectors do not create the mass employment needed by 1.4 billion Chinese.

\textbf{The digital palliative — Buying time.} To avoid social explosion, the Chinese State has deployed an algorithmic control system of unprecedented scope (social credit, e-CNY, flow regulation). This is not an end in itself, but a palliative intended to "freeze" the social situation while a real material solution is found.

\subsection{The real solution — The Territorial Regeneration Rent (TRR)}

This solution is already at work on the ground. Instead of continuing to concrete over virgin land, the State is massively injecting credit to regenerate the land degraded by forty years of hyper-industrialization, following the example of the Lishui pilot zone with the Two Mountains Bank. By restoring forests, soils and rivers, China is creating a new economic sector in its own right. Ecological restoration is becoming the new engine of local job creation.

\subsection{The TRR as the foundation of a new diplomacy}

Beyond China, the TRR founds a new diplomacy. By demonstrating that it is possible to exit the nodal phase without massive destruction of wealth, China offers the Global South a structural alternative to Western imperialism. This "Two Mountains diplomacy" positions the Economic Celestial Way (Tiandao Jingji, 天道经济) as a new viable civilizational standard, an alternative to the exhausted Western model.

\subsection{Strategic conclusion}

China has already diagnosed Stasis and begun to deploy the mechanisms of territorial regeneration — in Lishui, Sanming, Ganzhou, Hainan. This work proposes a mathematical formalization of this diagnosis and of this solution, as well as a steering apparatus for the whole of the integrated economy-geography.

The TRR is an operational application of discrete topology to the regulation of an economic system in crisis. It offers China a peaceful way out to avoid the tenth decline — the first time in two millennia that a Chinese state has at its disposal a tool to short-circuit the fatal cycle of dynastic collapses.

Chinese thought has been, since its origins, a science of navigation: knowing how to circulate and to balance between the yin and yang flows, whether to regulate the economy or to organize the territory (fengshui). The "Economic Celestial Way" (\textit{Tiandao Jingji}, 天道经济) mathematically formalizes this wisdom. It is neither an ideology nor a cultural metaphor, but the \textbf{topological path} strictly authorized by the Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$. It is the only transition trajectory that makes it possible to leave a saturated attractor (Stasis) in order to reach a new cycle of expansion, without triggering an unfavourable retropolarity (systemic collapse). The Tian Dao is the algorithmic expression of the nilpotency condition: it is the mathematical respect for this path that ensures the permanence of the Mandate of Heaven.

This work is addressed to curious minds — notably Eastern ones — custodians of the holistic correlative tradition, who will recognize in this apparatus a means of thinking and acting within integrated geo-economic complexity.

\section*{Foreword — The two levels of reading}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Foreword — The two levels of reading}

This document is structured into two levels of reading, intended for two different audiences.

\paragraph{Level 1 — The diagnosis and the solution (Parts I and III).}
Intended for decision-makers, strategists, political and economic leaders.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Part I}: The diagnosis of the Chinese structural crisis — the attainment of the nodal phase, Stasis, the dead end of the immaterial. Without equations. Without formalism. An economic, historical and strategic narrative.
\item \textbf{Part III}: The Territorial Regeneration Rent (TRR) as an operational solution — the mechanisms already at work in Lishui, Sanming, Ganzhou, Hainan.
\end{itemize}
The non-mathematical reader can read these parts without losing anything essential.

\paragraph{Level 2 — The topological model and its implications (Parts II and IV).}
Intended for theorists, mathematicians, epistemologists.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Part II}: The mathematical formalization of the model — the Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$, the 144 economic pentads, the 7 spectral thresholds, the transition operator $T$, the spectral observables.
\item \textbf{Part IV}: The philosophical and systemic implications — the economy as exosomatization of topology, Chinese correlative thought as a proto-model, divination as a pre-modern regulatory system.
\end{itemize}
The non-mathematical reader can skip these parts without losing the thread of the practical demonstration.

\paragraph{Status of this work relative to the Theory of Rent Extraction.}
It is important to specify the exact nature of this work relative to the original Theory of Rent Extraction (ToRE) of Thierry Rebour. This document does not merely \textit{apply} the ToRE to new historical cases: it proposes a \textbf{rigorous formal and mathematical extension} of it, carried out with the participation of Thierry Rebour. Where the original ToRE describes, in a qualitative and conceptual manner, the mechanisms of transfer from the Space of Value to the Space of Wealth, the present model transposes this dynamic into the framework of the Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$. This transposition makes it possible to \textit{quantify} the rupture thresholds, to \textit{identify} the stable states (attractors) and to \textit{model} the dynamic transitions, thereby transforming a descriptive geo-economic theory into an \textbf{operational and steerable discrete information system}. Moreover, this work algebraically formalizes the geographic aspect of the ToRE, raising it to the status of a genuine theory of the discrete topology of geo-economic spaces.

The document is articulated around five nested frameworks, each legitimizing the next. The reader is invited to keep this architecture in mind throughout his or her reading:

\part*{PART I — FROM THE THEORY OF RENT EXTRACTION TO CHINESE STASIS}
\addcontentsline{toc}{part}{PART I — FROM THE THEORY OF RENT EXTRACTION TO CHINESE STASIS}

## 0. Introduction

### 0.1. The observation: continuous models fail to predict crises

Since the publication of Keynes's *General Theory* (1936), macroeconomics has equipped itself with increasingly sophisticated mathematical tools. DSGE models (*Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium*), rational-expectations models, and Monte-Carlo simulations have become the standard instruments of central banks and ministries of finance.

Yet these models have systematically failed to anticipate the great crises of the 20th and 21st centuries: the Great Depression (1929), the oil shock (1973), the subprime crisis (2008), and more recently post-COVID inflation (2022). This failure is not accidental. It is **structural**.

Conventional models treat the economy as a continuous space, in which the variables (prices, wages, output, interest rates) adjust through mechanisms of convergence towards a supposed equilibrium. However, the Theory of Rent Extraction (ToRE), developed by Thierry Rebour [@rebour2000; @rebour2011], has shown that economic growth is fundamentally a phenomenon of **structural disequilibrium**, governed by conservation laws and discrete rupture thresholds: the Nodal Phases.

### 0.2. Epistemological prerequisite: why biology and linguistics?

The reader approaching this work for the first time may be surprised — even disconcerted — to see political economy set alongside the genetic code, Mandarin phonology or particle physics. This reaction is legitimate: it is the natural product of a modern Western epistemology that has founded its rigour on the specialization and compartmentalization of knowledge.

Yet the connections made in this work are neither poetic metaphor nor approximate analogy. They rest on a **rigorous mathematical isomorphism**: the topological invariant $64 \to 20$.

#### 0.2.1. The independence of the substrate

The fundamental discovery of contemporary theoretical physics — notably through Peter Rowlands's work on Clifford algebra — is that **complex information obeys the same topological stability constraints, whatever the physical substrate that carries it**.

When a system must encode, transmit and stabilize information in a noisy environment, it inevitably converges towards the same algebraic architecture. Nature does not reinvent the wheel at every scale: it reuses the same topological "source code".

- **In molecular biology**, the substrate is chemical (nucleotides). Topological filtration reduces the $4^3 = 64$ possible codons to the 20 stable amino acids needed to build proteins.
- **In linguistics (Mandarin phonology)**, the substrate is acoustic and articulatory. Filtration by the constraints of the vocal tract reduces the 64 syllabic combinations to the 20 fundamental phonological classes.
- **In economics and geography**, the substrate is social and material (value flows, territorial constraints). Filtration by the geometry of the Merkabah reduces the $2^6 = 64$ macroeconomic configurations to the 20 stable attractors.

#### 0.2.2. Internalization, symbolization, exosomatization

Rather than seeing these domains as foreign to one another, we must understand them as **three manifestations of the same underlying topology**, differentiated by their mode of expression:

1. **Biology (Internalization)**: the system encodes information *within itself* to ensure its survival and physical replication. This is the realm of DNA.
2. **Language (Symbolization)**: the system encodes information *between individuals* to ensure coordination and cultural transmission. This is the realm of Phonology.
3. **Economics (Exosomatization)**: the system encodes information *in material and social space* to ensure the allocation of resources and the regulation of groups. This is the realm of Institutions and of the Theory of Relative Scarcity.

Economics is therefore not a "soft" and isolated social science. It is a **physics of exosomatized symbolic systems**. Institutions, markets and borders are not purely arbitrary constructions: they are macroscopic projections of the same Clifford pentads which, at the microscopic scale, structure amino acids and phonemes.

#### 0.2.3. The light shed by Chinese correlative thought

For the reader familiar with the Chinese tradition, this unification is not a shock, but an obvious fact. Western thought seeks *causes* (linear, mechanistic: the analytics of forces) by reducing and simplifying questions until a fundamental causal link is brought to light (e.g. gravitation with Galileo).

Chinese thought seeks *correlations* (structural, topological: the dynamics of forms) aiming to unify all "regional ontologies" under the empire of a single structure (e.g. the Wuxing, which traditionally federates all levels of reality under the empire of a dynamics of 5 phases through which information circulates and regulates itself).

Likewise, the 64 hexagrams of the *Yi Jing* (Book of Changes) [@javary2002yijing] do not specifically describe the weather, war or agriculture: they describe the **64 fundamental states of information in mutation**, applicable to all domains of reality.

In the landscape defined by the Clifford algebras Cl(6,0) and Cl(6,6) where this work is situated, structures isomorphic to the concepts of traditional Chinese thought emerge spontaneously. Thus, Yi Jing, Wuxing and Bagua, algebraicized, are called upon to describe the structures of eco-geographic dynamics.

It is this profound unity that founds the legitimacy of the "Economic Celestial Way" (*Tiandao Jingji*, 天道经济): if the laws that govern matter, life and language are universal, then the laws that govern the economy must align with them in order to be enduring.

### 0.3. The hypothesis: the economy is a discrete information system

To bridge the gap between continuous models and the discrete reality of crises, we put forward the following hypothesis:

> **The economy is a discrete information system**, whose configuration space is isomorphic to the Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(6,0)$, and whose dynamics are governed by a universal invariant: the $64 \to 20$.

This hypothesis rests on three pillars:

1. **The formalism of Clifford algebras and nilpotent pentads**, developed by Peter Rowlands (2007, 2014). Rowlands has shown that the Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(6,0)$ decomposes into 12 pentads (sets of 5 elements, like the *Wuxing*), and that this pentad structure is fundamental for physics (the Dirac equation) as for biology. Our model transposes this architecture to economics: six binary dimensions — Inflation, Real wage, Profits, Rent extraction, Spatial dynamics, Land regime — generate $2^6 = 64$ possible states, exactly like the space of spins in quantum physics, the space of codons in biology, or the space of hexagrams of the *Yi Jing*.

2. **The substrate-independent generalization**, due to De Dominicis (2026). De Dominicis extended Rowlands's model by showing that the $\mathrm{Cl}(6,0)$ structure and the $64 \to 20$ invariant are not specific to physics or biology, but constitute a universal property of any complex system, whatever its substrate. It is this generalization that authorizes the transposition to economics.

3. **The exceptional lattice $\Lambda_{72}$**, constructed by Gabriele Nebe (2010). Nebe discovered an even unimodular lattice of dimension 72 whose 48 non-degenerate roots provide the fundamental resonance frequencies of complex systems. De Dominicis has shown that these 48 roots project onto a basis of 15 universal constants $\beta_k$, which are the same for nuclear physics, chemistry, biology and social systems.

### 0.5. Epistemological status of the model: a first approximation to be refined

The model presented in this work constitutes a **first approximation** of the discrete topology of complex economic systems. It is important to specify from the outset its status and its limits, in order to avoid any over-interpretation.

#### 0.5.1. The current granularity: 144 pentads for 1.4 billion agents

The $\mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$ model as developed here rests on 144 projected pentads (12 economic pentads $\times$ 12 geographic pentads). Relative to a Chinese economy of 1.4 billion agents, this represents a granularity of around **10 million people per pentad**.

This resolution is sufficient to capture **national macro-economic dynamics** and the great historical cycles (the 9 dynastic declines). It makes it possible to diagnose post-2018 Chinese Stasis, to identify attractor $S_{\text{eco}}$ as a blocked state, and to prescribe the Territorial Regeneration Rent (TRR) as a controlled transition operator.

However, this granularity is **insufficient** to:

- Capture regional heterogeneities (coastal/interior disparities)
- Model fine sectoral interactions (industry vs. services vs. agriculture)
- Steer policies at the prefectural or county scale
- Integrate local micro-frictions that may block or accelerate transitions.

The refinement trajectory is detailed in **Appendix T.4**.

#### 0.5.2. China as a laboratory: from national to local

China offers an ideal field of application for this refinement trajectory, because it already has:

- National macro-economic data (National Bureau of Statistics)
- Provincial data (31 provinces, autonomous regions, municipalities)
- Prefectural data (333 prefectures)
- County data (2,851 counties)

The current model has been calibrated on national data. The next step consists in **projecting the 144 pentads onto the 31 provinces**, using the adaptive dual-basis (Appendix T.2.3) to modulate the observables according to regional specificities. This will make it possible to:

- Identify provinces in advanced Stasis (e.g. Liaoning, Heilongjiang)
- Detect provinces in transition (e.g. Zhejiang, Guangdong)
- Adapt TRR policies to local contexts

#### 0.5.3. Falsifiability and open research programme

This refinement trajectory is not a mere technical sophistication. It is **necessary for the falsifiability of the model**:

- If the 144-pentad model fails to predict the regional transitions observed between 2026 and 2030, it will have to be revised.
- If the spectral observables ($\eta$, $d$, $\text{gap}$, $R_{\text{threshold}}$) do not capture inter-provincial imbalances, the projection onto bivectors will have to be accelerated.
- If the TRR deployed in Lishui does not produce the predicted spectral effects (crossing of $S_5$, decline of $\mathcal{I}_{\text{Stasis}}$), the model will have to be recalibrated.

The $\mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$ model is therefore not a **closed theory**, but an **open research programme** in the sense of Lakatos. It proposes:

- **A hard core**: the $64 \to 20$ invariant, nilpotency, the structure of the 20 attractors
- **A protective belt**: the spectral observables, the alert thresholds, the decision rules
- **Positive heuristics**: the extensions towards bivectors, trivectors, spinors

#### 0.5.4. What the model already delivers today

Despite its macroscopic granularity limits, the current model already provides powerful operational and epistemological tools:

1. **A structural diagnosis** of Chinese Stasis, going beyond classical conjunctural indicators (GDP, unemployment, inflation) to identify attractor $S_{\text{eco}}$ as a topologically blocked state.
2. **A topological prescription**: the TRR (Territorial Regeneration Rent) is identified as the only authorized unfolding operator for leaving Stasis without provoking an unfavourable retropolarity (collapse towards the 3N well).
3. **A multi-level dashboard**: based on the 144 fundamental geo-economic states, and extensible to the **66 tension observables** (bivectors) and **220 interaction observables** (trivectors). This makes it possible to steer imbalances finely without multiplying the states or breaking the $64 \to 20$ invariant.
4. **A qualitative confrontation**: the coherence of the model with the 9 Chinese dynastic declines and Western cycles (e.g. the Thirty Glorious Years), attesting to its temporal robustness.
5. **A unifying framework**: the demonstration that economics, biology, physics and linguistics obey the same topological invariant, economics being merely an exosomatized manifestation of this recurrent structural invariant.

Note: An unfavourable retropolarity is a direct, topologically forbidden transition between the expansion belts ($C_P$) and the recession belts ($C_N$) without passing through the polar thresholds ($P_4$ or $N_4$), provoking a systemic collapse (see formal definition in Chapter 14).

#### 0.5.5. Conclusion of Part I: a starting point, not an end

This work is therefore not a closed theory, but an **open research programme** in the sense of Lakatos. It proposes:

- **A hard core**: the $64 \to 20$ invariant, nilpotency, and the structure of the 20 attractors.
- **A protective belt**: the spectral observables ($\eta, d, \text{gap}, R_{\text{threshold}}$), the alert thresholds and the decision rules.
- **Positive heuristics**: the extensions towards bivectors, trivectors and pure spinors (detailed in Appendix T.4).

The future refinement of the model will not consist in stacking layers of "pentads" to gain resolution artificially (which would break the invariant), but in **unfolding the algebraic richness of $\mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$**: passing from the 144 fundamental states to the tensions (bivectors), then to 3-body interactions (trivectors), and finally to the internal symmetries ($SU(3) \times SU(3)$).

By opening the way to a general physics of discrete complex systems, this work presents a model of economic dynamics anchored in geographic territoriality. 
It makes it possible to discern the topological trajectory that allows navigation from a potentially catastrophic crisis situation towards a renewed positive dynamic.

But the millennia-old Chinese tradition has already empirically discerned these discrete topological dynamics, and this work merely confirms algebraically the diagnosis and the territorial regeneration programme already implemented by the Chinese authorities in several provinces, as described in **Part III**.

## Chapter 1 — Theoretical foundations: from the crisis of continuous models to the Theory of Rent Extraction

### 1.1. The observation: continuous models fail to predict crises

Since the publication of Keynes's *General Theory* (1936), macroeconomics has equipped itself with increasingly sophisticated mathematical tools. DSGE models (*Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium*), rational-expectations models, and Monte-Carlo simulations have become the standard instruments of central banks and ministries of finance.

Yet these models have systematically failed to anticipate the great crises of the 20th and 21st centuries: the Great Depression (1929), the oil shock (1973), the subprime crisis (2008), and more recently post-COVID inflation (2022). This failure is not accidental. It is structural.

Conventional models treat the economy as a continuous space, in which the variables (prices, wages, output, interest rates) adjust through mechanisms of convergence towards a supposed equilibrium. However, the **Theory of Rent Extraction** (ToRE), developed by the geographer-economist **Thierry Rebour** [@rebour2000; @rebour2011], has shown that economic growth is fundamentally a phenomenon of structural disequilibrium, governed by conservation laws and discrete rupture thresholds: the **Nodal Phases**.

\begin{tcolorbox}[
  colback=blue!5!white,
  colframe=blue!75!black,
  title=\textbf{Status of this work relative to the Theory of Rent Extraction (ToRE)},
  fonttitle=\bfseries
]

It is important to specify from the outset the exact nature of this work relative to the original Theory of Rent Extraction (ToRE) of Thierry Rebour. This document does not merely \textit{apply} the ToRE to new historical cases: it proposes a \textbf{rigorous formal and mathematical extension} of it.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Original ToRE \parencite{rebour2000, rebour2011}}: \textit{qualitative and conceptual} description of the mechanisms of transfer from the Space of Value to the Space of Wealth.
\item \textbf{Present model}: transposition into the framework of the Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$, making it possible to:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item \textit{quantify} the rupture thresholds,
  \item \textit{identify} the stable states (attractors),
  \item \textit{model} the dynamic transitions.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

This transposition transforms a descriptive geo-economic theory into an \textbf{operational and steerable discrete information system}.

Moreover, \textbf{with the direct participation of Thierry Rebour}, this work algebraically formalizes the geographic aspect of the ToRE, thereby raising it to the status of a genuine \textbf{theory of the discrete topology of geo-economic spaces}.

\end{tcolorbox}

### 1.5. The foundations of the Theory of Rent Extraction (ToRE)

Elaborated by Thierry Rebour [@rebour2000; @rebour2011], the ToRE models the sequence by which societies transform latent wealth into monetary wealth. It demonstrates that the power of growth rests on an initial structural asymmetry between two distinct conceptual spaces [@guieysse2016].

#### 1.5.1. Ontology of Value and Wealth

The ToRE divides the economy into two spheres of radically different nature [@rebour2000; @rebour2011]:

- **The Space of Value** does not designate simple unvalued assets, but assets kept outside the market by symbolic foundations and reasons more anthropological than economic. These are wealths "frozen" by sacralizations, collective beliefs or founding prohibitions that confer on these spaces an ontological thickness [@desmarais2000; @ritchotmercier1992].

- **The Space of Wealth** designates the monetized economic circuit, where these same assets, stripped of their symbolic veil, become factors of production generating prices, wages and profits [@rebour2000].

**Interpretation for China:** In the Chinese imperial matrix, land was the absolute Space of Value [@zhao2006tudi; @schmitt2017sol]. Under the Maoist era, collectivized land was a latent Space of Value of colossal size. In the *Tudi Caizheng* model (1978-2018), rural land, frozen by the *Hukou*, constituted a Space of Value that the State progressively transferred towards the Space of Wealth [@zhou2023liweilii; @chan2009hukou].

#### 1.5.2. The mechanism of rent extraction and money creation

Rent extraction is the act of transferring an asset from the Space of Value to the Space of Wealth. This transfer requires a political or social decision that lifts the original prohibition [@rebour2000].

However, since the asset is not yet productive at the time of transfer, the purchaser does not possess the income necessary to pay for it. Financing can therefore only occur through monetary anticipation: rent extraction is intrinsically linked to the creation of money through credit. As the theory stipulates, material rent extraction is always "made solvent by an act of money creation, in other words, a loan" [@rebour2011].

**Interpretation for China:** The LGFVs (*Local Government Financing Vehicles*) were the instrument of this anticipatory credit. By borrowing massively from state banks, the municipalities created the money necessary for land rent extraction [@zhou2023liweilii; @chen2024; @mof2023lgfv].

#### 1.5.3. Advance exogenous demand

The injection of credit intended for rent extraction does not descend into the real economy at the same time as the new assets enter production: it precedes it. This advance exogenous demand translates into a new purchasing power (compensation, construction wages, land profits) injected before the new means of production become operational [@rebour2000].

This structural lag generates price inflation (notably of land) that rises faster than labour income. Growth is thus fundamentally in disequilibrium or polarized: it structurally advantages rent-holders at the expense of wages [@rebour2011; @rebour2011a].

#### 1.5.4. Increasing returns and territorial multipliers

Although it is born of a disequilibrium, this sequence generates real prosperity. Exogenous demand concentrates capital and activities in a single place. This spatial concentration generates positive externalities (networks, know-how, infrastructure) that increase overall productivity. The profits earned are reinvested, creating multiplier effects [@rebour2000; @desmarais2000].

#### 1.5.5. The substitution of externalities

This process of concentration is not without spatial cost; it is governed by a strict law of substitution of externalities [@rebour2000; @desmarais2000; @ritchotmercier1992]. To understand its mechanism, we must return to its historical roots. This phenomenon is not due to a simple monetary transfer, but to a productivity shock — initially agricultural — that makes viable the relocation of productive tasks towards the countryside. This is the very principle of the *Verlagsystem* (putting-out system): production is externalized in rural spaces, while the city retains strategic control (design, financing, marketing) and captures the essential part of the surplus value generated. From then on, metropolitan prosperity has nothing of endogenous growth: it is the accounting reflection of the impoverishment of the peripheries [@rebour2011a].

#### 1.5.6. The nodal phase

The ToRE being governed by conservation laws (Value is not created *ex nihilo*, it moves), the cycle of growth in disequilibrium is limited by the nodal phase [@rebour2011]. This systemic threshold is reached when the stock of easily mobilizable Value runs out. The flow of credit intended for rent extraction dries up, depriving the economy of its "advance exogenous demand". Inflation slows, asset prices stagnate, and increasing returns give way to diminishing returns [@rebour2000; @rebour2011].

#### 1.5.7. The conservation law and centrifugal dynamics

At the nodal phase, the crisis is not an anomaly, but the system's obligatory readjustment mechanism: to recreate Value, one must destroy Wealth (bankruptcies, deindustrialization, price collapse) [@rebour2011]. The ToRE insists on a morphological corollary that is often ignored: the attainment of the nodal phase reverses spatial dynamics [@rebour2011a; @desmarais2000]. The growth period polarized space towards the centre (centripetal dynamics). At the nodal phase, the dynamics become centrifugal. We observe diffuse periurbanization, de-urbanization of centres, and an inversion of urban hierarchies. The crisis is therefore as much financial as morphological [@ritchotmercier1992].

This resolution is sufficient to capture national macro-economic dynamics and the great historical cycles (the 9 dynastic declines). #### 1.6.2. The limits of the model and future work

Macroscopic granularity is not the only limit of the current model. Three other structural limits must be signalled:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Provisional calibration}: the weights $w_i$ of the composite Stasis index are calibrated on the 9 Chinese dynastic declines. Their validity for other cultural contexts remains to be tested.

\item \textbf{Imperfect data}: the observables of Level 4 (geo-economic states) and of Level 5 (inter-pentad relations) require fine data that are not always available at the required scale.

\item \textbf{Non-linearities}: the model assumes linear relations between the observables. Threshold effects and bifurcations are not fully captured by the current formalism.
\end{enumerate}

These limits define an \textbf{open research programme} in the sense of Lakatos, articulated around three priorities:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Exhaustive empirical validation}: test the $64 \to 20$ projection on an expanded corpus of 20 to 30 historical regimes (Appendix N, §N.8).
\item \textbf{Operationalization of bivectors}: define quantitative indicators for the 66 tensions $\mathcal{T}_{ij}$ (Appendix T, §T.4).
\item \textbf{Inter-cultural extension}: apply the model to other world-systems (Rome, medieval Europe, Latin America) to test the universality of the invariant.
\end{itemize}

For a complete presentation of the refinement trajectory (from the 144 states to bivectors, trivectors and spinors), the reader is invited to refer to \textbf{Appendix T, §T.4}.

## Chapter 2 — The Chinese Imperial Matrix: A Multi-Century Trend from Antiquity to the Present

### Introduction — A Single Trend, Two Modes of Value

The history of imperial China is traditionally interpreted through the prism of Confucian morality (the ruler's virtue), palace intrigues, or social class analysis. Yet, if we set aside the chronological narrative and apply the framework of the Theory of Rent Extraction (ToRE), the two millennia of dynastic cycles appear as the repeated implementation of an inexorable economic deadline [@elvin1973pattern; @zhao2006tudi; @perkins1969agricultural]. The succession of Chinese dynasties does not correspond to a succession of independent economic trends. From the formation of agrarian civilisation to contemporary China, it is a **single multi-century trend**, of which the successive dynasties constitute successive historical configurations.

The fundamental mechanics of this trend rest on the law of unbalanced growth [@rebour2000]. The rent extraction process transfers land (or labour power) from the Space of Value to the Space of Wealth, in exchange for a monetary payment (borrowing) that anticipates future production. This influx of "exogenous" demand, occurring ahead of the production cycle, drives prices up faster than incomes, generating an inflationary growth trend. Within this polarised regime, profits and rent mutually sustain one another, supported by increasing returns, while the purchasing power of wages tends to erode.

The system's operation then depends on the relative scarcity of two fundamental modes of Value: **land Value** and **the Value of servile labour power**. When labour power is scarcer than land, the system is in a **pioneer front** situation. When land becomes scarcer, the system shifts towards **land rent**. Chinese history can thus be understood as a succession of shifts between these two modes, accompanied by avoidance mechanisms designed to postpone the deadline of the nodal phase.

### 2.1. The Two Fundamental Modes of Value

#### 2.1.1. The Landed Mode and Agrarian Ontology

To understand the application of ToRE to China, it is necessary to grasp the specific nature of its relationship with land. Although Europe also experienced a long period of domination by the landed aristocracy (feudalism), China's trajectory is distinguished by the bureaucratic centralisation of rent. In China, land was not merely a factor of production, but the foundation of imperial legitimacy (the Mandate of Heaven) and the ultimate refuge for the capital of the scholar-official elites.

Unlike the West, where feudal fragmentation eventually gave way to the commodification of land (*enclosures*) and the rise of a merchant bourgeoisie capable of challenging the supremacy of the landed aristocracy, China maintained a "state agrarian ontology" into the modern era. Within this system, genuine Wealth did not arise from autonomous market exchange, but from control over the soil and the peasantry by the state apparatus [@granet1922religion; @schmitt2017sol; @zhao2006tudi]. It was this immobilisation of land within the Space of Value, under state control, that constituted the vast reservoir mobilised during the post-1978 Rent Extraction process.

Within this paradigm, land is not simply a factor of production; it is the absolute Space of Value. However, for rent to be extracted from it, this land must be kept outside a free market and subjected to a political prohibition.

This is where China innovated long before the industrial era: through draconian control over peasant mobility (the conceptual ancestors of the Hukou system). By binding peasants to the land, the imperial state secured a captive workforce and a perfectly stable stock of Value [@fei2013xiangtu; @vandermeersch1980wangdao].

China's distinctive feature, therefore, was not that it sacralised land (as feudal Europe also did), but that it prevented the emergence of an independent landed aristocracy and a merchant bourgeoisie powerful enough to challenge the imperial order. Land remained the absolute Space of Value, fully controlled by the state, until Deng Xiaoping's reforms lifted the economic prohibition while maintaining the political prohibition (through the Hukou system).

In a sedentary society, access to land becomes the principal factor of economic differentiation, making rent extraction possible. This phenomenon has a crucial consequence: **the Wealth produced by labour does not disappear, but an increasing share of that Wealth is transferred to the holder of the land rights**. The system thus tends towards concentration.

#### 2.1.2. The Servile Mode

The situation is radically different when land is relatively abundant but labour power is scarce. The system must then **capture labour power from outside the market circuit** in order to feed the Space of Wealth. This capture can take two historically distinct, but structurally isomorphic, forms:

- **External mooring (military conquest):** in antiquity, the capture and enslavement of exogenous populations directly supplied the labour power required by the pioneer front. The holder of capital (the state or the landowner) directly owns the productive capacity of the worker's body itself.
- **Internal mooring (institutional confinement):** in contemporary China, the **Hukou** (residential registration system) performs precisely the same structural function, without military conquest. By tying social rights to the rural place of origin and prohibiting permanent migration, it artificially maintains a mass of migrant peasants in a status of captive quasi-proletarians — neither fully wage-earners (without urban rights) nor fully peasants (without effective access to land). Their labour power is thus **frozen in the Space of Value** until the state decides to redeem it at a marginal cost close to zero.

In both cases, the slave or proletarianised migrant peasant constitutes a labour force whose productive capacity is directly appropriated by its holder, without the latter having to bear the full cost of its social reproduction. The **pioneer front** thus emerges as the configuration in which territorial expansion and the expansion of the stock of servile labour power operate jointly.

### 2.2. The Two Crisis-Avoidance Mechanisms and the Nodal Phase

The dynamics of rent extraction generate growth that inevitably encounters the limits of effective demand, threatening to trigger crises of overproduction. To prevent prices from collapsing, the system has two avoidance mechanisms at its disposal.

The first, **spatial avoidance**, consists in pushing the system's limits further through geographical expansion or exports. Chinese history provides a paradigmatic illustration of these avoidance loops: one province exports to another in order to avoid local overproduction. But when the loop closes, once goods have circulated through all the provinces, there is nowhere left to export to. This is when the global crisis breaks out.

The second, **temporal avoidance**, postpones the constraint into the future through the use of money, credit, and debt. Nevertheless, this artifice does not create new real resources. The gap between monetary Value and the productive base widens, preparing the ground for financial crises.

These mechanisms make it possible to postpone the **nodal phase**. In theory, the latter occurs when all land is on the market, but in reality, in unbalanced economies, it occurs as soon as **more than half of the stock of Value has been redeemed** and Wealth (production) becomes greater than Value. Since prices are no longer stimulated by the release of Value, they stagnate. To restore price increases, **Wealth Destruction** and the correlative recreation of Value become indispensable. Returns then become diminishing: the economy turns into a zero-sum game, marking the entry into a prolonged "Crisis" [@rebour2011; @elvin1973pattern].

### 2.3. The Spatial Laws of Rent Extraction: Urban Form and Externality Substitution

The relationship between the modes of Value and the economic conjuncture determines spatial organisation. An inflationary growth trend generates centripetal dynamics and increasing returns that polarise space.

In a pioneer front situation, cities adopt an orthogonal geometry (rectangular grid), visible in ancient China, Rome, and under the Tang and Yuan dynasties. According to Naba-Chen theory, these grid plans, introduced by nomadic peoples, reflect the influence of a servile mode reintroduced through conquest [@shatzman-steinhardt1988].

When the pioneer front closes and land becomes scarce, the logic changes. To maintain profits in the face of insufficient domestic purchasing power, developed cities must maximise their exports. Spatial attractors then become axial: cities expand in "arms" along communication routes. This is the law of externality substitution: Value is transferred from the countryside to the cities. Appropriation did not proceed through brute force, but through the structural asymmetry of agricultural markets: the forced indebtedness of peasants in the face of rigid taxation, combined with the "price scissors" imposed by elites monopolising grain storage, systematically transferred Wealth from the countryside to the centres [@rebour2011a; @huang1974taxation].


### 2.4. Ancient China: From Available Land to Land Rent

Chinese growth truly began with the Shang dynasty (around 2500 BCE). During the early phases, available space made it possible to maintain a pioneer front. However, population growth and the integration of territories gradually reduced this margin. China then entered a land-rent regime. This transformation marked the locking-in of the trend. Political crises were no longer the end of a system, but manifestations of the same problem: how could rent extraction continue when land resources became insufficient?

### 2.5. Qin and Han: Centralisation, Land Registration, and the Locking-in of the Trend

The Han (from 300 BCE to 300 CE) underwent a structural nodal phase. Land rent extraction accelerated. The Han brought slavery to an end, introduced rigorous land registration, and closed the pioneer front. Value became structurally tied to land. This transition can be read in the spatial configuration: cities ceased to follow a grid pattern, signalling the abandonment of pioneer-front geometry in favour of rent-based polarisation. Land concentration generated the tensions that led to the crisis at the end of the Han period (the Yellow Turban Rebellion of 184), the first major manifestation of the exhaustion of the land regime [@elvin1973pattern; @zhao2006tudi].

### 2.6. The Five Barbarians (Fourth–Fifth Centuries): Wealth Destruction and Spatial Division

The fall of the Han and the Three Kingdoms period marked the onset of the nodal phase: extreme land concentration, collapsing demand, and a crisis of overproduction. To escape this crisis, the system resorted to massive **Wealth Destruction** through civil wars. But it was the arrival of nomadic peoples, known as the "Five Barbarians" (*Wu Hu*), in the fourth century that made it possible to restart the trend.

The conquest of northern China by these non-Chinese peoples brought about a violent redistribution of the Space of Value. The settled landed elites were decimated or fled southwards, leading to the division of the empire. In the North, the new nomadic rulers founded the Sixteen Kingdoms and then the Northern Dynasties. They massively reintroduced the **servile mode**: Chinese peasant populations were often enslaved or bound to the land under semi-servile status in order to cultivate the estates of the nomadic military aristocracies. The pioneer front and Value based on labour power were reactivated.

In the South, the Southern Dynasties (Eastern Jin, Liu Song, etc.) pursued **spatial avoidance** by pushing the agricultural frontier towards the Yangtze regions and bringing new land into cultivation. This geographical division between the fourth and fifth centuries illustrates one way of resolving a crisis: the North shifted towards the servile mode through conquest, while the South sought a new land-based pioneer front.

### 2.7. Nomadic Invasions and the Reactivation of the Pioneer Front

When the land system reaches a high level of concentration, it eventually implodes under the weight of overproduction and falling prices. The Chinese state attempts to control prices, preventing wages from adjusting downwards quickly enough. Through greed, the state and the aristocracy raise taxes. Excessive predation prevents the economy from recovering, while inequality leads to looting and civil wars.

This is where the dynamics of nomadic invasions play a role in macro-historical regulation. Every new dynasty rises from the ashes of Wealth Destruction. The new ruling house undertakes a large-scale redistribution of land confiscated from the former elites. The Space of Value is suddenly redistributed [@huang1974taxation; @yang2015tangdai]. Nomadic peoples enter China, seize power, redistribute land, and restart a growth trend. Their arrival brings about **Wealth Destruction** (which recreates Value) and reintroduces servile labour power. The pioneer front temporarily reappears. The process begins again under the Sui and Tang. The nomads become sinicised, adopt agrarian institutions, and turn into predatory rent extractors: land concentration begins once more.

### 2.8. Tang and Song: Expansion, Grid Planning, and Spatial Saturation

The Tang restored a powerful empire. The Silk Road constituted a vast episode of spatial avoidance. The urban grid pattern reappeared in Xi’an/Chang’an and Luoyang (seventh century). But expansion eventually reached its limits: the land constraint resurfaced with the An Lushan Rebellion (755) [@twitchett1970financial; @yang2015tangdai].

Under the Song, land was structurally scarce and spatial avoidance was insufficient. The system shifted massively towards **temporal avoidance**. Fiat currency (*jiaozi*) and maritime trade mobilised future Wealth. But money cannot create land. The gap between monetary value and the real productive base eventually erupted in financial crises.

### 2.9. The Jurchen (Jin Dynasty, 1120–1250): Division of the Empire and the Duality of the Modes of Value

Before Mongol unification, China experienced another division, illustrating the duality of the ToRE's avoidance mechanisms. In the twelfth century, the Jurchen (Jin dynasty, 1115–1234, occupying the period 1120–1250) seized northern China, bringing the Northern Song to an end in 1127.

This incursion once again brought about **Wealth Destruction** in the North. The Jurchen, a nomadic people, imposed a mixed system: they confiscated land belonging to Chinese elites and allocated it to their military aristocracy, while reducing part of the peasantry to semi-servile status (the *meng'an* and *mouke* systems). The pioneer front and the servile mode were thus reactivated in the northern half of the country.

The South (the Southern Song, 1127–1279), deprived of territorial expansion, entered a phase of hyper-specialisation in **temporal avoidance**. The regime's survival depended on an explosion in fiat currency, credit, and large-scale maritime exports (porcelain, silk) to compensate for the loss of the Space of Value. China was divided between a North (Jin) based on coerced labour power and a South (Song) suffocating under debt and monetary inflation. It was against the backdrop of this exhausted duality that the Mongols (Yuan) would impose unification through widespread Wealth Destruction.

### 2.10. Yuan and Ming: From the Return of the Pioneer Front to Institutional Stasis

The Mongol conquest (Yuan) reintegrated China into a vast Eurasian empire, reactivating the pioneer front (the grid layout of Beijing in the thirteenth century). But the conquerors settled down, became sinicised, and land rent once again prevailed [@elvin1973pattern].

The Ming inherited a saturated system. Temporal avoidance gained importance with the influx of exogenous silver, but this did not change the amount of land. Above all, the Ming introduced a fatal rigidity: **they refused to sell land to peasants in full ownership**, which would have made it possible to restart rent extraction. This rigidity led to institutional **stasis**. Peasant indebtedness and land concentration culminated in the Li Zicheng Rebellion and the Manchu invasion [@huang1974taxation].

### 2.11. Qing, Republic, and Mao Era: From the Last Spatial Frontier to the Freezing of the Trend

The Qing undertook the last major territorial expansion (Xinjiang, Tibet, Taiwan), the final great episode of spatial avoidance. But in the nineteenth century, external space became insufficient. The land constraint once again became overwhelming (the Taiping Rebellion), while Western pressure imposed structural indebtedness [@perkins1969agricultural]. The nodal phase of the imperial matrix had been reached.

The collapse of 1912 and the Republic did not create a new trend: fragmentation, hyperinflation, and the absence of any rent-extraction mechanism marked the terminal Crisis [@elvin1973pattern].

The Mao era constituted a political rupture, but inaugurated an **artificial stasis** in the sense of the ToRE. Collectivisation removed land from the market, while the *Hukou* system froze mobility. The rent-extraction system was **frozen**. Land and labour power became stocks of latent Value whose mobilisation was institutionally prevented.

### 2.12. Deng Xiaoping: Acceleration of the Trend and Mobilisation of the Latent Stock

The 1978 reforms represented the **reactivation of the old trend**. The difference lay in the speed at which the latent Value accumulated over centuries was mobilised.

Urbanisation massively transformed rural land into urban real estate. The continued existence of the *Hukou* system made it possible to control the mobility of a low-cost workforce, sustaining rents and profits. Land became the basis for a gigantic conversion of Value, financed by massive temporal avoidance (credit, LGFVs). China abruptly accelerated the old trend towards its limit.

### 2.13. Synthesis of the Nine Declines: The Standardised Dynastic Matrix

The analysis of the nine major periods of decline confirms the validity of this model while revealing two adjustment variables: labour scarcity and exogenous shocks [@elvin1973pattern; @perkins1969agricultural; @twitchett1970financial; @huang1974taxation]. ### 2.14. The Terminal Nodal Phase and the Trimorphy of Chinese Space

The contemporary period is characterised by the simultaneous saturation of both avoidance possibilities. Spatial avoidance no longer has a pioneer front; temporal avoidance (debt) can no longer replace a real Value base. China has reached its **terminal nodal phase**.

Today, China's geographical space reflects this situation of diminishing returns through the **trimorphy of space** [@rebour2011]:

- **Metropolitan spaces** (hypertrophied): capital intensity can still overcome the rent constraint by building upwards, attracting selective global demand.
- **Urban spaces**: where rent blocks the growth of cities in proportion to their size.
- **Rural spaces**: impoverished by externality substitution in favour of metropolitan areas, and affected by the atrophy of their capital.

In previous crises, Wealth Destruction (civil war, invasion) made it possible to alter the scarcity ratio. Today, this possibility is structurally limited. Repeating the old mechanism would lead to **Stasis**, in a zero-sum game.

### 2.15. Territorial Regeneration Rent: Exiting the Trend

It is in this context that **Territorial Regeneration Rent (TRR)** acquires its significance.

In the old system, Value is obtained by mobilising a resource that is already available. At the nodal phase, the only option open to capital is Wealth Destruction in order to recreate Value. TRR proposes an alternative: **the regeneration of a degraded space itself becomes a source of Value**.

Space becomes an object capable of qualitative transformation. TRR would therefore not constitute another episode in the avoidance spiral, but the first attempt to **exit the historical trend based on scarcity and the appropriation of existing resources**, replacing destruction with endogenous Value creation.

### Conclusion — The Nodal Phase as a Historical Rupture

Chinese history appears as a single trajectory oscillating between land Value and servile Value, shaped by externality substitution and avoidance mechanisms. For centuries, dynastic crises and nomadic invasions made it possible to destroy Wealth in order to recreate Value and postpone the nodal phase.

Mao suspended the mechanism through institutional stasis. Deng reactivated it at an unprecedented speed, consuming the last stocks of latent Value. The contemporary period corresponds to the simultaneous exhaustion of spatial and temporal avoidance.

The historical question is no longer how to restart the next cycle through destruction, but whether it is possible to **exit the trend itself**. This is precisely the theoretical function that Territorial Regeneration Rent could fulfil. Contemporary China therefore faces a historical alternative: **continue the avoidance spiral until Stasis is reached, or transform the very principle of rent extraction by generating qualitative Value.**
