## Chapter 3 — The Western Interruption: The Banking and Industrial Escape Route

While imperial China spent two millennia repeating a closed land-based cycle, the West found, for a time, a way to circumvent the laws of the Theory of Rent Extraction (ToRE). By observing the mechanism of the nodal phase—the exhaustion of the Value stock leading to Wealth Destruction—Europe and then America developed a systematic avoidance strategy. They succeeded in postponing the fatal deadline by artificially broadening the very definition of what could be "subject to rent extraction", and by inventing the financial machinery capable of making this expansion solvent [@rebour2000; @elvin1973pattern; @fourastie1979].

### 3.1. Industrial Rent Extraction: The Sudden Expansion of the Value Stock

In the Chinese imperial matrix, the Space of Value was finite and bounded: arable land. Once all the land had been redistributed and then appropriated, the nodal phase became inevitable [@elvin1973pattern; @rebour2000].

The Western innovation of the Industrial Revolution was economic rather than technological: it consisted in opening up new Spaces of Value. The subsoil (coal, followed by oil and minerals) and the machine itself were "frozen" assets, either because they could not technically be exploited or because property rights had not been clearly established [@rebour2000; @fourastie1979].

Industrial rent extraction was the political and economic act of transferring assets from the Space of Value to the Space of Wealth. Unlike Chinese land, which was static, this new Value was dynamic: technological innovation continuously created new underground frontiers or new machines to be subjected to rent extraction. This shift gave the West the illusion that it had overcome diminishing returns [@rebour2011; @fourastie1979].

### 3.2. International Banking as a Means of Making Assets Solvent

However, the ToRE lays down an immutable rule: transferring an asset into the Space of Wealth requires "advance exogenous demand". Yet, when a factory is being built or a coal mine opened, the asset is not yet productive. Who pays? [@rebour2000]

This is where the financial layer comes in. The West innovated by institutionalising money creation through private credit (and subsequently international banking). The major banking houses of London, Amsterdam, and later New York provided the monetary anticipation required for industrial rent extraction. The money lent to build infrastructure or factories was spent immediately (wages, profits), generating the structural inflation characteristic of the polarised ToRE regime [@rebour2011; @griffin2010creature].

For this system not to collapse under the weight of its own inflation, however, it constantly needed new spaces in which to sell its output and absorb imbalances. This mechanism of externality substitution, initially confined to the European countryside, was taken beyond its original spatial framework by international finance. In the nineteenth century, international finance funded the relocation of production and the extraction of raw materials to the "global countryside" constituted by the colonies [@rebour2011a; @griffin2010creature].

### 3.3. The First Global Nodal Phase (1914–1945)

Under the law of conservation, the expansion of the Space of Value through industry and finance could only be temporary. By the end of the nineteenth century, the entire Earth had been surveyed, mapped, and colonised. There were no longer any "virgin lands" or unclaimed subsoil resources to feed the rent-extraction machine. The global stock of Value suddenly became saturated, marking the arrival of a nodal phase on a civilisational scale [@rebour2011; @fourastie1979].

The ToRE thus explains what conventional historiography persists in treating as mere diplomatic accidents: the First World War, the Great Depression, and the Second World War were, in reality, the compulsory and violent adjustments of the global financial and industrial system to this critical threshold. The law of rent extraction required massive Wealth Destruction in order to recreate Value [@rebour2011; @lewin1996report].

The West had temporarily diverted the cycle by opening it up on a global scale. But when it closed that cycle (once colonisation was complete), it was hit full force by the law of conservation that had reduced Chinese dynasties to ashes for centuries. The only difference was that this time the adjustment took place on the scale of the entire industrial civilisation [@rebour2011; @fourastie1979].

---

## Chapter 4 — China 1978–2018: The Golden Age of Material Rent Extraction

China's take-off from the 1990s onwards illustrates the ToRE sequence: a vast stock of land Value outside the market, the lifting of the prohibition and the triggering of rent extraction through anticipatory credit, followed by the generation of increasing returns.

### 4.1. The 1978 Reform and the Lifting of the Maoist Prohibition

To launch a rent-extraction cycle, a vast stock of frozen Value is required. Under the Mao era (the period before the reforms), land and the means of production were collectivised. They were not operated according to market laws, but neither were they sacralised by an ancestral anthropological prohibition: they were simply "frozen" by inefficient planning, forming a latent Space of Value of colossal size [@chan2009hukou; @zhao2006tudi].

Deng Xiaoping did not privatise the land (which would have undermined political control). He lifted the economic prohibition while maintaining the political prohibition. The **Hukou** (household registration system) played the same role here as peasant status had under the Tang or Qing: it artificially kept the rural workforce and land within the Space of Value, preventing them from being freely traded on the market [@chan2009hukou; @zhang2012model].

The reform consisted in authorising the transfer of *land-use rights* (not ownership) over collectively owned land to operators or municipalities. This was an unprecedented form of rent extraction: China mobilised land without transferring full ownership, thereby creating the conditions for a captive land rent for the state [@zhao2006tudi; @long2018chuantong].

### 4.2. The Hukou as a Political Operator of Rent Extraction

The rent-extraction mechanism requires a stock of Value that has been politically frozen. The fundamental specificity of the Chinese model lies in the architecture of its property regime, a duality often poorly understood through Western analytical frameworks. As the political theorist Zhang Weiwei points out, the Chinese model rests on the fact that "the state owns most resources, from minerals to land, but land-use rights are flexible and shaped by market forces" [@chan2009hukou].

For the "flexibility" of land-use rights to generate maximum rent during rent extraction, however, the state's ownership of the original stock had to remain strictly locked in. It was precisely at this micro-level that the Hukou system operated [@chan2009hukou]. By tying social rights (healthcare, education, housing) to the rural place of origin and prohibiting permanent migration to cities, the system artificially kept rural land and labour power within the Space of Value.

When municipalities subsequently decided to initiate rent extraction, the acquisition price of this rural land—deprived of any legal liquidity by the Hukou system—was kept close to zero. This artificial gap made it possible to maximise the rent captured by the state when land-use rights were resold to property developers, thereby initiating the exogenous-demand cycle.

This capture of land rent was accompanied by an equally decisive demographic externalisation. By locking in the Hukou system, the cost of the social reproduction of labour power was shifted onto the countryside. Migrant workers, deprived of access to urban public services, relied structurally on the families they had left in their villages to care for children, the sick, and the elderly. The village therefore supplied not only a stock of rural land to be expropriated at a zero marginal cost; it also subsidised, free of charge, the reproduction costs of the urban workforce. This dual extraction—land-based and social—made it possible to keep construction wages artificially low, maximising the rent captured by the state through the LGFVs and accelerating the exogenous-demand cycle.



### 4.3. Externality Substitution on a Continental Scale

Unlike the West, which externalised its costs towards the Global South, the Chinese cycle **internalised** externality substitution within its own borders:

- "Wealth" became concentrated along the coastal seaboard (the Special Economic Zones), capturing export value added.
- "Costs" (the ageing of an unintegrated workforce, ecological degradation, and a lack of social services) were externalised to the inland regions and the countryside.

This spatial asymmetry made it possible to maintain double-digit growth rates for three decades, with the system absorbing its own contradictions through the sheer extent of its territory.

### 4.4. The Party-State as the Central Bank of Rent Extraction: LGFVs

In the Western model (Part I, Chapter 3), private banks created money to make industrial rent extraction solvent, capturing a share of the rent in the process. China bypassed this process. The Party-State became its own banker [@rebour2000].

Unable to borrow directly on the markets (or able to do so only to a very limited extent at first), municipalities created *ad hoc* financial vehicles: **LGFVs** (Local Government Financing Vehicles), 城投债 (*Chengtouzhai*). These entities, implicitly guaranteed by the state, borrowed on a massive scale from state-owned banks [@mof2023lgfv; @imf2023china; @chen2024].

The financial engine of this period rests on a remarkable form of topological anticipation. Municipalities, as the exclusive owners of the land, expropriated agricultural land at low prices (latent Value) and rezoned it for construction (monetised Wealth). By using land as collateral for large-scale borrowing, LGFVs injected colossal amounts of liquidity into the economy *before* the infrastructure had even been built. This is the exact embodiment of the concept of "advance exogenous demand" theorised by Rebour. The strategic state acted as the **central bank of rent extraction**, transforming future land rent into present fixed capital (motorways, high-speed railways, and ports).

#### 4.4.1. Material Rent Extraction and the Collectivisation of Rent

This money was used to expropriate peasants (at a price close to zero, thanks to the freezing effect of the Hukou system) and to finance infrastructure. The sums paid to peasants and construction workers immediately entered the real economy: this was the pure embodiment of the **"advance exogenous demand"** theorised by the ToRE. The resale of land-use rights by the Party-State generated colossal profits, which were used to repay LGFVs and finance new projects. The cycle of unbalanced growth (land-price inflation exceeding wage growth) was set in motion.

It is, however, essential to distinguish this recycling of rent from imperial predation or Western fictitious finance. Unlike dynastic elites, who hoarded agrarian rent, or financial markets, which channelled it into speculative assets, the Party-State collectivised this rent in order to convert it into territorial capital. Mega-infrastructure (high-speed railways, dams, and energy transfers) is not a by-product of growth: it is its physical materialisation, realising the increasing returns and territorial multipliers described by the ToRE. This tangible conversion of land extraction into collective assets explains the model's lasting legitimacy.

Nevertheless, the law of conservation implies that, in doing so, the state was silently preparing the conditions for its own nodal phase. By building this infrastructure ahead of actual demand in order to sustain exogenous demand, it accumulated a colossal stock of assets which, in time, risked turning into financial liabilities if they failed to generate the future rent required to repay LGFV debt.

#### 4.4.2. The Structural Dead End: The LGFV Crisis

LGFVs are the central instrument of this rent extraction, but also its weak point. Created by local governments to circumvent the prohibition on direct borrowing, they backed their debt with the future value of land. This mechanism rests on a structural contradiction: local governments are both the masters of their LGFVs and their prisoners. They control them (shareholdings, appointment of executives, access to land collateral), but are captive to the implicit guarantee that obliges them to support them whatever happens—especially since the collapse in land revenues has dried up their main source of repayment.

To conceal the arrival of the nodal phase, the system generated a dual structure of debt: official debt, recorded on balance sheets and subject to Beijing's quotas, and hidden debt, contracted off balance sheet. This concealed debt made it possible to maintain credit flows artificially for years, until the collapse of the land market brought it into the open.

Faced with systemic risk, Beijing launched a broad effort to reassert control: tighter supervision, a ban on implicit guarantees, and the forced transformation of LGFVs into commercial entities. But this process faces an inexorable reality: LGFVs are too heavily indebted to be abandoned (without triggering immediate Wealth Destruction), yet too fragile to be rescued without creating massive moral hazard. It is precisely this deadlock—the impossibility of allowing the system to collapse and the impossibility of maintaining it in its current form without sinking into fictitious Wealth—that constitutes the concrete expression of China's nodal phase. The "Wealth Destruction" theorised by the ToRE takes here the anticipated form of a forced debt restructuring [@imf2023china; @mof2023lgfv].

Three conventional ways out of the crisis are theoretically available to Beijing for absorbing this surplus Wealth, but each proves structurally incapable of restarting the cycle:

- **Debt swap (controlled evanescence):** Beijing would require state-owned banks to exchange their short-term claims for very long-term, low-yield sovereign bonds. In ToRE terms, this amounts to destroying future rent without destroying the physical asset. Although this solution preserves apparent capital, it freezes the system in a form of **financial Stasis**: deprived of returns, banks lose their capacity to make new cycles solvent, dragging the economy into a Japanese-style zombification that does not resolve the nodal phase but freezes it indefinitely.
- **Selective default (surgical destruction):** This approach would consist in imposing a *haircut* on creditors of certain LGFVs, or even allowing the most insolvent entities to fail. This is the purest form of Wealth Destruction—the targeted modern equivalent of the peasant revolts of earlier times. However, the risk of systemic contagion is considerable: a partial default could trigger a generalised liquidity crisis, as investors withdraw their funds pre-emptively from the entire local financial system.
- **Monetary inflation (dilutive erosion):** The People's Bank of China could create money on a massive scale to buy back LGFV debt, thereby eroding the value of Wealth through dilution. But resorting to inflation is the quintessential Western approach. In China, increases in retail or property prices have historically triggered dynastic collapses. This represents an absolute political risk for the Party-State, potentially destroying its own legitimacy before the nodal phase has even been addressed.

If the debt swap leads to Stasis, default to contagion, and inflation to social risk, these three paths share one fatal characteristic: they are sterile. They manage the evaporation of Wealth, but **none recreates the stock of Value** required to initiate a new cycle.

It is precisely this structural dead end that makes the activation of **Territorial Regeneration Rent (TRR)** unavoidable. To prevent unproductive Wealth Destruction, the state must force the emergence of a new rent-extraction cycle by backing existing debt with an underlying asset capable of generating real rent.

### 4.5. The Rent Extraction of Geography: Mega-Infrastructure and Externality Substitution

China's achievement during this period was to understand that the Space of Value was not limited to agricultural land on the outskirts of cities (which would eventually be exhausted). It transposed the concept of rent extraction to **physical geography itself** [@zhang2018bilu; @rebour2000].

Western history had mobilised the subsoil and the colonies. Unable to colonise abroad, China colonised its own landlocked interior. The mega-infrastructure projects of the 1990s and 2000s were the instruments of this geographical rent extraction:

#### 4.5.1. The Three Gorges Dam

The Yangtze River was more than a transport route; it was a wild "Space of Value", whose devastating floods represented periodic Wealth Destruction, while its energy and hydraulic potential remained entirely inaccessible because of the technical and financial impossibility of mobilising it.

The decision to build the dam fits the pure rent-extraction mechanism. Through a massive political act, the state lifted the natural prohibition, mobilising colossal credit (more than 200 billion yuan at the time) to "buy" the riverbed. This injection of capital generated phenomenal "advance exogenous demand" for nearly twenty years, supporting the national heavy industry (cement, steel, and civil engineering) at a time when the domestic market had not yet fully developed.

However, the ToRE analysis above all reveals **externality substitution on an unprecedented scale**. The dam was not built to enrich the Three Gorges region (Hubei/Chongqing), which paid an exorbitant price for the operation: more than one million people displaced, historic towns submerged, and ecosystems destroyed. The hydroelectric power generated and flood control benefits were captured for the exclusive benefit of the eastern coastal metropolises (the Yangtze River Delta).

The metropolitan centre (Shanghai and, more broadly, the entire export-oriented maritime seaboard) was thus able to industrialise at breakneck speed thanks to abundant, cheap, and stable electricity "imported" from the heart of the continent. The prosperity of the metropolitan Space was built on the physical and social atrophy of the middle Yangtze valley.

Finally, the Three Gorges Dam acted as the fundamental hydraulic hub of the Yangtze basin: without its reservoir to regulate flows across seasons, the South–North Water Transfer Project (analysed in 4.5.3) would have been technically unfeasible. The dam thus marks the culmination of the Party-State's capacity to reshape the country's physical geography in order to force the abstraction of resources for the benefit of increasing returns.

#### 4.5.2. The West–East Gas Pipeline

While the Three Gorges Dam enabled hydraulic regulation, the West–East Gas Pipeline (*Xiqi Dongshu*) served a parallel and independent purpose: energy substitution. The manufacturing prosperity of the coastal regions (Shanghai, Jiangsu) required cheap energy that local coal could no longer provide without undermining profitability (pollution, logistical costs). By "extracting rent" from western gas (Xinjiang), the Party-State substituted the periphery's energy externality for the benefit of the centre (the Yangtze River Delta).

The gas from the Taklamakan Desert represents a weak externality (a resource without access infrastructure), not a strong externality (Value frozen by a symbolic prohibition). The term "rent extraction" is used by analogy with the ToRE, but, strictly speaking, the operation is a conventional infrastructure investment.

The account of the decision to build the West–East Gas Pipeline perfectly illustrates the theoretical sequence of the morphogenetic process specific to Structural Geography:

- **Aesthetic (Tianxia):** The Reform Architect's geopolitical vision of drawing a line "with a bold and colourful brushstroke" (浓墨重彩) from west to east across the map of China, in order to open up the development of the West, was not merely a calculation of profitability, but an expression of territorial harmony inspired by cosmology [@zhang2018bilu].
- **Political (the property rule):** The Reform Architect—representing the CCP—makes the sovereign decision to lift the geographical prohibition. At the operational level, Zhang Guobao, head of the Planning Commission (NDRC), acts as the technical operator of rent extraction: he mobilises state credit, imposes the network despite local resistance (e.g. the Rice Province), and overrides the warnings of experts (CIECC), validating the political act through empirical rigour.
- **Economic (rent extraction, by analogy):** Massive financing through state debt creates "advance exogenous demand" (through the construction of the infrastructure).

This case demonstrates that the Chinese model was neither a simple "free-market miracle" nor orthodox centralised planning, but the systematic application of the laws of the ToRE on a continental scale. The Party-State acted as the ultimate capitalist entrepreneur, "extracting rent" from geography itself in order to initiate a new cycle of unbalanced growth.

#### 4.5.3. The South–North Canal (South–North Water Transfer)

The prosperity of the northern metropolises (Beijing, the Northern City) encountered an absolute physical limit: the depletion of groundwater. Meanwhile, the Yangtze River basin, regulated by the Three Gorges Dam, had surplus water. Water, a natural element, had become an asset "frozen" by geography: it existed, but it was in the wrong place.

The South–North Canal project fits the rent-extraction mechanism. The Party-State mobilised colossal credit to "buy" this distance of more than 1,000 kilometres. From the perspective of the ToRE, this is the most extreme illustration of externality substitution: the survival and growth of the political centre (Beijing) were made possible by drawing on the water capital of the southern periphery. The North extracted rent from the South's vital resource, perpetuating Northern overaccumulation at the expense of regional balance, while generating the exogenous demand associated with construction of the canal.

#### 4.5.4. Maritime Access Canals (e.g. the Pinglu Canal)

The second project concerns opening up mountainous hinterlands to the sea, with the Pinglu Canal (South-West Province) being the largest example. Historically, the provinces of the South-West had to transport their goods eastwards to reach the sea via the Pearl River Delta (Shenzhen). This dependence created an overwhelming locational rent for the eastern coastal metropolises.

The south-western hinterland occupied the typical position of an "atrophied Space": its productive externalities were captured by the centres located along the flow corridors. To counter this centrifugal dynamic, the Party-State decided to extract rent from topography by digging a canal through the mountains to connect inland rivers directly to the Gulf of Tonkin.

This project reveals a sophisticated use of the ToRE at the end of the cycle. It involves **artificially injecting a maritime externality into the periphery** in order to restart a micro-cycle of rent extraction there. By giving the South-West Province direct access to the sea, the Party-State creates a new local land and logistics rent. The credit injected into excavation generates exogenous demand, while the infrastructure is intended to attract factories, thereby recreating increasing returns locally in a region threatened with economic downgrading.

### 4.6. Exhaustion of the Geographical Pioneer Front and the Emergence of "Refractory Values"

Far from marking the limits of the ToRE, these final projects instead confirm its predictive validity: **material rent extraction itself is coming to an end**. The marginal return on these operations is falling sharply. The South–North Canal entails increasingly heavy negative externalities (the drying up of the lower Yangtze) that destroy Value in the donor periphery [@chen2026phosphorus]. The Pinglu Canal requires colossal investment (giant locks, tunnels) for an increasingly uncertain economic benefit compared with the railway network.

The exhaustion of land finance (readily available urban land) drove the Party-State to extract rent from the subsoil (gas), then from the river (Three Gorges), then from inter-basin water systems (South–North Canal), and finally from topography (Pinglu). Yet each new instance of rent extraction required more credit to generate lower real productive returns.

Although some physical spaces remain technically exploitable (hydroelectric power in Tibet/Qinghai, geothermal energy in Xinjiang), the costs of extraction and infrastructure, together with the environmental externalities, are so high that they can no longer generate the increasing returns required by the rent-extraction cycle. In accordance with the law of diminishing returns inherent in the ToRE, the marginal cost of rent extraction eventually exceeds the marginal value of the Wealth produced.

As a hypothesis, we propose extending the law of conservation of Value by classifying these territories as **Refractory Values**: they physically exist, but the economic laws of the system mean that integrating them into the productive circuit would require the destruction of more Wealth than it would create, thereby blocking the rent-extraction process. This is a theoretical extension, not a concept found in the original ToRE corpus.

### 4.7. Topological Trajectory of the 1978–2018 Cycle: Evolution of the Pentads

The narrative analysis of the four decades of material rent extraction must be supplemented by a fine-grained topological reading: each phase of the cycle corresponds to a dominant **triplet of economic pentads** and a **triplet of geographical pentads**, which define the attractor in which the system evolves. This reading in terms of activated pentads reveals the underlying logic of the cycle and anticipates its breaking point.

#### 4.7.1. Methodology: Temporal Reading of the Pentads

At each instant \(t\), the Chinese geo-economic system can be projected onto:

\begin{itemize}
\item The space of the 20 economic attractors $\mathcal{A}_{\text{eco}}$ through the local observables $\eta_k^{(\text{eco})}(t)$ for each pentad $P_k$ or $N_k$
\item The space of the 20 geographical attractors $\mathcal{A}_{\text{geo}}$ through the local observables $\eta_j^{(\text{geo})}(t)$ for each pentad $G_j$ or $H_j$
\end{itemize}

Pentads whose activity satisfies $a_k(t) > 0.5$ and whose asymmetry satisfies $|\eta_k(t)| > 0.3$ are considered **dominant**. Their combination defines the system's dominant attractor at time \(t\).

The actual economic trajectory of the Chinese cycle passes only through \textbf{structurally active cells} and traces a \textbf{turning-back movement}:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Ascent (1978–2008):} from \textcolor{green!70!black}{\textbf{Li × Water}} (attractor $D_{\text{eco}}$, moderate growth) towards \textcolor{blue!80!black}{\textbf{Qian × Wood}} (attractor $B_{\text{eco}}$, polarised export-led expansion), then \textcolor{orange!90!black}{\textbf{Qian × Wood}} (attractor $A_{\text{eco}}$, extreme expansion). The system reaches its maximum structure (Qian = high inflation, wages, and profits), with active rent extraction (Wood). This is the peak of rent extraction. A \textbf{topological degeneracy phenomenon} occurs between phases 2 and 3: the trajectory remains in the same cell but changes attractor (from $B$ to $A$).
\item \textbf{Diagonal descent to the left (2008–2015):} from Qian × Wood towards \textcolor{purple!80!black}{\textbf{Li × Metal}} (attractor $H_{\text{eco}}$, rentier economy). The system retains the Li structure but moves down one phase (Wood → Metal), signalling the transition from active rent extraction to rent extraction in a saturated territory (Oecumene).
\item \textbf{Diagonal crossing (2015–2018):} from Li × Metal towards \textcolor{red!90!black}{\textbf{Kun × Fire}} (attractor $S_{\text{eco}}$, economic Stasis). The system crosses the grid towards the minimum structure (Kun), with dispersion (Fire). This movement reveals that Stasis corresponds to the topological opposite of the peak (minimum structure + dispersion).
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}

\item \textbf{Return and trap (2015–2018):} a \textbf{fascinating topological phenomenon}: the trajectory returns to the \textcolor{red!90!black}{\textbf{Qian × Metal}} cell, but the attractor becomes $S_{\text{geo}}$ (territorial Stasis). Enclosure ($H_5$) isolates a network which, deprived of its macrocephalic driving force, stagnates in a static equilibrium ($H_6$). The maximum geographical structure (Qian), which had been the cycle's energy peak, has become a trap.
\end{itemize}

This divergence is the signature of the duality $\mathrm{Cl}(6,0)_{\text{eco}} \otimes \mathrm{Cl}(0,6)_{\text{geo}}$:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Economic dimension:} the exhaustion of the Value stock translates into a collapse of the structure (Qian → Kun). The system "lets go".
\item \textbf{Geographical dimension:} the exhaustion of the Value stock translates into a \textbf{structural lock-in} (Qian remains Qian, but becomes a trap). The territory remains frozen in its most concentrated form, unable to generate new pioneer fronts.
\end{itemize}

Nevertheless, the two trajectories converge towards the same diagnosis: **geo-economic Stasis** ($S_{\text{eco}} \times S_{\text{geo}}$), confirming the validity of the cross-diagnosis presented in Chapter 16.

\subsubsection{4.7.6. Synthesis: The Topological Logic of the Cycle}

The analysis in terms of activated pentads reveals that the Chinese cycle from 1978 to 2018 is not a simple linear growth process, but a \textbf{structured topological trajectory} across the two subspaces:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Opening} (1978–1990): the system evolves within an attractor of moderate growth ($D_{\text{eco}}$) and a dynamic pioneer front ($E_{\text{geo}}$), with an orthogonal spatial form (O+) typical of SEZs.
\item \textbf{Acceleration} (1990–2008): the system shifts towards attractors of polarised expansion ($B_{\text{eco}}$ then $A_{\text{eco}}$ on the economic side; $C_{\text{geo}}$ then $A_{\text{geo}}$ on the geographical side), with a radial and then concentric form encoding the export of surpluses followed by metropolitan polarisation.
\item \textbf{Drift} (2008–2015): the system moves towards a rentier economy ($H_{\text{eco}}$) and a constrained metropolis ($D_{\text{geo}}$), with a concentric form (C+) encoding the shift towards reliance on domestic rent.
\item \textbf{Collapse / Entrapment} (2015–2018): the system shifts towards Stasis ($S_{\text{eco}} \times S_{\text{geo}}$). On the economic side, the structure collapses towards Kun (minimum). On the geographical side, the structure remains locked into Qian (trapped maximum). The form becomes fragmented (F), signalling geo-economic Stasis.
\end{enumerate}

This trajectory is \textbf{topologically inevitable}: once the land Value stock has been exhausted (Phase 5), the system can no longer generate "advance exogenous demand" through material rent extraction. It is mathematically compelled to shift towards Stasis, unless the transition operator $T_{\text{mixed}}$ (TRR) intervenes, enabling a controlled passage through threshold $N_4$.

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=blue!5!white,colframe=blue!75!black,title=In a Nutshell]
The Chinese cycle from 1978 to 2018 is the purest historical manifestation of the Theory of Rent Extraction: a system that evolves topologically from an expansion attractor ($D_{\text{eco}} \times E_{\text{geo}}$) towards a Stasis attractor ($S_{\text{eco}} \times S_{\text{geo}}$), successively activating pentads $P_4$ (Exports), $P_3$ (Indebtedness), $P_1$ (Keynesianism), and then $N_5$ (Stasis), with a spatial form evolving from O+ to C+ and then F, thereby fully validating the $\mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$ formalism.
\end{tcolorbox}

## Chapter 5 — The exhaustion of the multi-century trend and its consequences

If the Hukou froze labour and rural land, another stock of Value, of a different nature but subject to the same laws, had remained outside the market: disconnected territories and immobilized energy resources. As the memoirs of Zhang Guobao, the principal architect of these projects, recall, the gas of the Xinjiang desert was "burned in the air" (the "lights in the sky") because no market existed to absorb it [@zhang2018bilu]. Within the framework of the ToRE, this enclaved physical space (the 4,000 km between Xinjiang and Shanghai) and this non-market resource constituted an immense geographic Space of Value, which the subsequent mega-infrastructure would progressively extract. However, this territorial expansion, however colossal, was bound to meet a limit.


\subsection{5.1. Exhaustion of the stock of land and geographic Value}

The quantitative exhaustion of mobilizable assets triggers the nodal phase theorized by the ToRE.

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=blue!5!white,colframe=blue!75!black,title=Formal diagnosis]
The complete spectral diagnosis of post-2018 China — binary configuration $\mathbf{x} = (0,0,0,0,1,0)$, projection onto attractor $S = \{P_6, N_5, N_6\}$, and dominant geo-economic state $N_5 \otimes H_5$ — is presented exhaustively in \textbf{Chapter 16, §16.1}. The reader will also find there the validation tables (Tables \ref{tab:configuration_chine_cl60} and \ref{tab:configuration_chine_cl06}).
\end{tcolorbox}

The saturation of real estate and the halt of mega-infrastructure are therefore not conjunctural accidents: the cycle of material rent extraction is interrupted by the simultaneous exhaustion of the land and geographic Space of Value, and the nodal phase is reached.

This tension between the physical exhaustion of assets and the State's logic of anticipation had already manifested itself during the design of the West–East Gas Pipeline. Experts from the International Engineering Consulting Corporation (CIECC) had assessed the proven reserves and recommended a capacity of 120 billion m³, judging the risk of 200 billion too high. Zhang Guobao, acting as the operator of rent extraction, had opposed this, arguing that a strategic project of this magnitude should "leave a margin" to anticipate future imports of Central Asian gas [@zhang2018bilu]. This conflict was not technical but structurally linked to the ToRE: the experts reasoned in "equilibrium" (proven value = capacity), while the Party-State reasoned in "disequilibrium" (future value must be anticipated through credit in order to maintain exogenous demand). The fact that Zhang "yielded" before the experts (reduction to 120 billion) marks a first sign of the weakening of the Party-State's capacity to force rent extraction beyond physical limits, a prelude to the nodal phase where the Wealth created no longer suffices to justify indebtedness.

### 5.2. Morphological manifestations of the nodal phase: ghost cities, exo-regulated dispersion, inversion of hierarchies

The ToRE insists on a corollary often ignored by purely macro-economic analyses: at the nodal phase, spatial dynamics invert, and the hitherto centripetal mobility — whether endo-regulated (gathering) or exo-regulated (concentration) — gives way to a centrifugal mobility: escape (endo-regulated) for the affluent classes, and **dispersion** (exo-regulated) for populations forced to leave saturated centres under the pressure of costs and the shortage of affordable housing [@rebour2000, sec. 3.3]. The saturated metropolitan space expels the vital forces towards the periphery.

This is exactly what is observed in China with the "ghost cities" (such as Kangbashi in Ordos) [@wu2015ghost]. These new cities built far from historical centres are not simple local "planning errors"; they are the spatial manifestation of exo-regulated dispersion. Capital, no longer finding profitability in the centres (diminishing returns), deployed towards virgin peripheries in a desperate attempt to recreate a local rent-extraction cycle. The inversion of urban hierarchies — with the relative decline of certain hyper-centres in favour of rank-2 or rank-3 cities during a short period — confirms that the Chinese territory has entered the morphological crisis phase of the ToRE.

The morphology of these ghost cities is not accidental. The ToRE distinguishes two great families of urban forms [@rebour2000, sec. 3.1-3.3]:

- **centred forms** (circular, concentric) are associated with regimes of distributive maturity, and proceed from an endo-regulated mobility (chosen gathering); - - **eccentric forms** (sectorial, axial) are associated with regimes of polarized growth, and proceed from an exo-regulated mobility (concentration undergone along the export axes).

Chinese new cities like Kangbashi, built *ex nihilo* along communication axes and disconnected from historical urban fabrics, are archetypes of the eccentric form arising from exo-regulated concentration. Their failure to attract a durable population and economic activity is not a simple planning defect; it is the spatial manifestation of a polarized growth that has reached its term. The maintenance of these eccentric forms after the nodal phase signals that the transition towards a regime of distributive maturity has not taken place: the cities have not recentred on poles of domestic consumption, but have remained oriented towards axes and nodes whose economic function has died with the end of polarized growth.

This morphological observation is illuminated by the regulatory role of rent on urban hierarchies, as analysed by the ToRE [@rebour2000, sec. 2.2]. In the ascending phase of the cycle, land rent blocks the growth of cities proportionally to their size: the larger a city, the higher the rent, and the more it discourages marginal investments, redirecting them towards the lower echelons of the hierarchy. This mechanism generates the rank-size harmonic function, where each city finds its place in a balanced hierarchy [@rebour2011a].

In China, this mechanism has been neutralized by spatial flows of capital (the LGFVs, State investments), which have allowed metropolises to overcome the rent constraint by accumulating fixed capital (skyscrapers, infrastructure). But at the nodal phase, when these flows dry up, the regulatory logic of rent reappears — but in the opposite direction. Rank-3 and rank-4 cities, which have never benefited from sufficient capital accumulation to overcome their rent, see their rent too low to retain the capital fleeing the metropolises. They cannot absorb the dispersion, because their low rent does not generate sufficient externalities to attract investment. Morphological dispersion is thus doubled by a blocked urban hierarchy: the metropolises retain their speculative rent (even when disconnected from use value), while medium and small cities remain structurally incapable of retaining the vital forces.

This hierarchical blockage has a direct consequence on the metropolises themselves. If rank-3 and rank-4 cities cannot absorb the dispersion, the capital fleeing them also finds no productive outlets in the metropolises. Speculative rent remains high there, but it is no longer supported by solvent demand. Vacant offices multiply in the CBDs, retail businesses close for lack of customers, and commercial surfaces degrade into urban wastelands.

This phenomenon is the physical manifestation of the **disconnection between rent and use value** that the ToRE identifies as characteristic of the nodal phase [@rebour2000, sec. 2.6]. Rent is no longer the product of a productive dynamic; it is fixed by speculation on a finite stock. The metropolises retain their skyline and their skyscrapers, but these "ghost" infrastructures now house empty spaces: the verticality that was the sign of overaccumulation becomes the symbol of its exhaustion.

### 5.3. The sovereign destruction of parasitic Wealth: the "Three Red Lines" and the Evergrande precedent

The conservation law of the ToRE stipulates that at the nodal phase, a destruction of Wealth is necessary to recreate the conditions of a new cycle. In Western economies, this destruction occurs chaotically through the market: cascading bankruptcies, price collapse, mass unemployment, socialization of bank losses (the 2008 scenario). The Party-State, strong in its capacity for strategic coordination, has chosen a radically different path: **selective sovereign demolition**.

The policy of the "Three Red Lines" (三条红线), triggered in August 2020, illustrates how the Party-State took control of the management of overaccumulation, refusing to delegate it to market forces alone. By imposing strict debt ratios on real-estate developers, the Party-State orchestrated a targeted reduction of the sector's overcapacity.

The case of **Evergrande** illustrates the logic of this structural selection. The group had massively indebted itself on the Hong Kong offshore markets, issuing dollar-denominated bonds and thereby integrating the Chinese real-estate sector into the sphere of international financialization. This connection constituted a transmission channel for extraterritorial risks: in the event of a cycle reversal, foreign creditors could have exerted destabilizing pressure on the domestic financial system. By allowing Evergrande to default on its offshore debt while prosecuting its executives for embezzlement, the Party-State carried out a triple structural adjustment:

1. **Sanctioning of rentier drift:** the destruction of the developer's shareholder and financial Wealth, reaffirming that virtuous legitimacy (*De*) prevails over speculative private profit;
2. **Monetary and geopolitical firebreak:** the cutting of the contagion channel of Western financial speculation, protecting the domestic banking system from the extraterritoriality of the dollar and immunizing the Chinese cycle against the Federal Reserve's rate cycles;
3. **Preservation of the social contract:** through the slogan *Baojiaolou* (保交楼 — "Guarantee housing delivery"), the Party-State split Wealth into two components. It sacrificed financial Wealth (the *offshore* creditors, the shareholders, the executives), but mobilized public resources to complete the construction of the housing pre-sold to households. Use value — the concrete territorial anchoring of the family in its home — was protected in the name of virtuous legitimacy (*De*), while speculative Wealth was delivered to destruction.

This sequence can be interpreted as an illustration of the logic of the ToRE in its political dimension: the destruction of Wealth at the nodal phase is *obligatory* within the theoretical framework, but its modality — chaotic through the market or sovereign through the Party-State — depends on institutional and political structures. Where the West socialized bank losses to save the financial system in 2008, China made the opposite choice, sacrificing the developers to save households and preserve the social contract. This difference does not validate the theory, but illustrates a possible application within a specific institutional context.

However, the ToRE teaches that the destruction of Wealth is only the first half of the nodal-phase equation. For the cycle to restart, this destruction must release capital towards a *new* rent extraction, a new Space of Value capable of generating advance exogenous demand. Now, by destroying the model of off-plan real-estate sales — which rested on households' confidence in future delivery — the Party-State simultaneously dried up the historical mechanism of local money creation. The selection eliminated the parasite, but the patient is left paralysed. Local governments, already asphyxiated by LGFVs, find themselves facing a vacuum of exogenous demand that neither classical bank credit nor central budgetary transfers manage to fill. It is this structural dead end, and not a diagnostic error, that makes the search for a new pioneer front imperative.

### 5.4. The closure of internal material frontiers and the necessity of a Third Mutation

Faced with this blockage, the Party-State faces the theoretical alternative of the nodal phase: let the destruction of Wealth occur in an uncontrolled manner (the Western scenario), or find a new pioneer front capable of recreating mobilizable Value. The virtuous discernment of the Party-State through the **Three Red Lines** has treated the first half of the equation; it remains to identify the new stock of Value.

The analysis of Chinese investments abroad must distinguish two structurally different categories. The transport corridors of the Silk Roads — gas pipelines, pipelines, railways, maritime routes — are transit infrastructures that secure physical flows between China and world markets. Their profitability does not depend on local sovereignty: the West–East Gas Pipeline, the Central Asia–Europe railways and the Russia–Empire pipelines remain operational because they are backed by guaranteed flows and strategic corridors.

By contrast, local productive investments — HPAL plants in Indonesia, the port of Chancay (Peru), the port of Hambantota (Sri Lanka), the port of Piraeus (Greece) — present a mixed record. The ports, designed as port Hardened Enclaves (§5.5.5), have succeeded: they benefit from exclusive rights, regulatory exemptions and total collateral that make any expropriation economically destructive for the host. Processing plants, on the other hand, are structurally vulnerable to the **Sovereignty Rent**\footnote{The "Sovereignty Rent" designates the economic value attached to a State's capacity to unilaterally modify the rules of the game on its territory (quotas, exchange rates, taxation). It is activated when the host State modifies the operating conditions of a foreign asset. Hardened Enclaves are designed to immunize investments against this rent.} of the host State: Indonesian decree No. 144 (2026) demonstrated that a sovereign State can unilaterally modify the rules of the game (quotas, costs, currencies), rendering the Chinese financial arrangement untenable [@esdm2026decree144; @scmp2026indonesia].

The lesson of the Third Mutation is that China now privileges logistical enclaves (ports, pipelines) over processing plants, because the former are immunized against the Sovereignty Rent of host States. The external material pioneer front is therefore practically closed for industrial processing, but still open for logistical enclaves — a distinction that Chinese strategy has integrated. If the Silk Roads infrastructure has partially succeeded in organizing the spatial flows of the Tianxia [@cai2021bri], it has not generated the "advance exogenous demand" necessary to absorb the shock of the domestic nodal phase. The economic returns of external investments in processing prove too weak and too slow to compensate for the brutal halt of the internal land engine [@hurley2019docking]. The external material pioneer front being practically closed for industry, the systemic constraint tightens.

It is in this context that the strategic planning capacity of the unified Party-State finds itself confronted with its deepest epistemological limit. The epistemology of the infinite development of productive forces collides with the conservation law of the ToRE: the stock of Value is *finite* at a given moment of technology and geography. The interregional coordination capacity that made it possible to build ultra-high-voltage networks, high-speed railways and inter-basin water transfers cannot, by itself, *create* a new stock of Value where physical geography no longer offers one. The Party-State can coordinate, plan, distribute; it cannot decree the existence of a virgin Space of Value once the territory has been entirely extracted.

To maintain the Mandate of Heaven and preserve the social harmony founding the "De", the Party-State is therefore constrained to operate a radical internal shift. The "Third Mutation" towards the immaterial (carbon, life data, sovereign artificial intelligence) is neither a headlong flight nor a denial of reality: it constitutes the most ambitious sovereign attempt to *transcend* the conservation law by creating new normative scarcities, in order to avoid the social cost of a generalized material destruction that the implicit contract between the Party-State and the population renders politically unacceptable. It is this systemic constraint — the necessity of recreating a rent-extraction cycle without disposing of a new geographic substrate — that justifies the launch of this mutation and that constitutes, simultaneously, its structural limit, as will be demonstrated in Part III.

### 5.5. The externalization of the destruction of Wealth and the structural dependence of the periphery

The Third Mutation, analysed in its immaterial dimension, raises an operational question: how does China ensure its supply of material substrates (minerals, energy, components) while its domestic economy has entered Stasis? The answer lies in a transformation of the role of the periphery in the global economic system.

#### 5.5.1. The geographic externalization of the destruction of Wealth

The ToRE teaches that at the nodal phase, material Wealth must be destroyed so that rent can be recreated elsewhere (cf. §1.4.7). In the Western historical model, this destruction struck centre and periphery indiscriminately. China, by escaping into the immaterial, has modified this given.

The Chinese strategy consists in **relocating part of the destruction of Wealth** towards the host States of its external investments. This mechanism is not a malicious intention, but a structural consequence of the asymmetry between Chinese assets (immaterial, immunized) and assets located abroad (physical, vulnerable). China can repatriate its strategic equipment and its technologies, leaving the host with unfinished or inoperative infrastructure. The devaluation of assets is thus geographically localized on the territory of the host, not on that of the centre.

This transfer is not a deliberate design but a structural property of the system: Chinese immaterial assets (tokens, quotas, exploitation rights) are immunized against physical shocks, while material assets located abroad are exposed to them. This structural asymmetry makes the periphery more vulnerable to devaluation cycles than the centre.

#### 5.5.2. The costs and limits of withdrawal

It would however be erroneous to think that China emerges unscathed from these withdrawals. The dismantling of the HPAL plants of Sulawesi in 2026 led to real losses: the loans of the CDB and the Export Bank remain largely unrepaid, future cash flows are lost, and China's image as a reliable partner has been tarnished. China has certainly repatriated its titanium autoclaves and its know-how, but it has lost several billion dollars of investment and a strategic position in the nickel supply chain. Indonesia, for its part, has lost plants that it cannot operate without Chinese reagents and engineering, but it has preserved its sovereignty over its resources — a non-negligible political gain.

The case of Venezuela offers an instructive parallel. Beijing had granted massive loans to Caracas (more than 50 billion dollars between 2007 and 2015), secured against oil deliveries. The collapse of the Venezuelan economy and political instability led to a renegotiation of the debt: China had to accept losses, reschedulings and a reduction of its claims [@hurley2019docking]. The Sovereignty Rent of the host State was activated, not by a decree, but by institutional collapse, which made debt service impossible. China could not seize Venezuelan oil assets without risking definitively compromising its relationship with a strategic partner. It therefore had to absorb part of the destruction of Wealth.

The difference with Indonesia lies in the nature of the asset: the HPAL plants were localized assets, partly seizable; Venezuelan oil is an underground asset, less easily transferable. But in both cases, China suffered losses. The asymmetry is therefore not absolute: it is a structural bias that, on average, protects the centre, but not a total immunity.

#### 5.5.3. Debt as an instrument of structural dependence

China finances its external investments through loans from the CDB and the China Exim Bank secured against the future cash flows of the projects (cf. §4.3.2). This arrangement, similar to the land finance model, works as long as the host State does not exercise its **Sovereignty Rent** — that is to say, its capacity to unilaterally modify the rules of the game (quotas, exchange rates, taxation). When Jakarta activated this rent via decree No. 144, the financial arrangement collapsed. China had to withdraw, leaving Indonesia with unfinished infrastructure and unpaid debts, but itself bearing part of the cost.

The lesson has been integrated by Beijing: future investments must be designed to be more resilient to the host's Sovereignty Rent. This is the logic of the **port Hardened Enclaves** (cf. §5.5.5) — de facto extraterritorial infrastructures, protected by exclusive rights, regulatory exemptions and total collateral that make any unilateral modification of the rules economically destructive for the host. This lesson was partly drawn from the Indonesian and Venezuelan withdrawals: where the host can modify the rules, China must lock its positions through legal and financial architecture, not through political trust.

Chinese external debt is therefore not an instrument of a "debt trap" but a **mechanism of structural dependence**. It creates an asymmetry in which the host State bears the essential part of the devaluation risks, while the Chinese centre retains control of the normative assets that guarantee the debt. This asymmetry, however, has limits: if losses accumulate (Venezuela), China is forced to absorb them, which reduces the scope of externalization.

#### 5.5.4. Agricultural externalization: leased land in Russia and global agro-industrial partnerships

Since the 2010s, China has engaged in a strategy of externalizing agricultural production onto vast expanses of under-exploited land abroad. This strategy, which is part of a logic of securing food supplies, takes various forms depending on the regions and institutional contexts.

**The Russian case: the long-term lease model**

The areas leased or controlled by Chinese interests in Russia exceed 670,000 hectares (according to SIPRI estimates), and could reach more than one million hectares according to more recent sources, including 426,600 hectares in direct lease near the border. The terms of these leases are precise: 49-year contracts, annual rent of 300 to 600 yuan per hectare, and the obligation to employ at least 30% Russian labour. Production (soybean, wheat, maize, meat) is partly exported to China, contributing to the country's food security, which is only 50% self-sufficient in soybean.

**The other agricultural fronts: Africa, Latin America and Southeast Asia**

Beyond Russia, China has deployed a global strategy of agricultural investment, often described as "going out" in the agri-food sector. The main investment foci include:

- **Sub-Saharan Africa**: China is active in several countries, with varied intervention models. In **Madagascar**, cooperation mainly concerns technology transfer (hybrid rice) and public-private partnerships, without massive land leasing. Memoranda of understanding have been signed to increase cultivable areas, but the Chinese commitment remains focused on mechanization and training. In **Angola**, a 130,000-hectare project is dedicated to soybean and maize cultivation, 60% of whose production is intended for export to China. In **Tanzania**, Chinese companies have developed projects on 32,000 hectares. In **Zambia**, investments have been made on land leased for 99 years. In the **Democratic Republic of the Congo**, a 2.8-million-hectare project is planned for a palm oil plantation. Other projects exist in **Senegal**, **Sierra Leone** and **Mozambique**.

- **Latin America**: China has invested in agricultural land in **Brazil**, **Argentina** and **Uruguay**, mainly for the production of soybean, maize and cereals. These investments are often made through trade agreements or stakes in local companies, rather than through direct leases.

- **Southeast Asia**: Investments have been made in **Laos**, **Cambodia**, **Thailand** and **Myanmar**, where Chinese companies cultivate rice, rubber and energy crops (sugarcane, palm oil).

**ToRE typology of Chinese agricultural partnerships abroad**

Within the framework of the Theory of Rent Extraction, these operations are radically distinct from the Chinese land model. **This case illustrates a weak externality (an under-exploited resource without access infrastructure or without access to markets)**, not a rent extraction in the strict sense of the ToRE. Unlike Chinese land, foreign land is not "frozen" by an anthropological or symbolic prohibition. It is simply under-used and subject to sovereign regulation. China leases, it does not buy; it produces, it does not speculate.

\textbf{The Sovereignty Rent and the dialectic of controlled solvency}

In all cases, the host States retain the entirety of their
\textbf{Sovereignty Rent}: they can at any time modify the terms of the
leases, increase rents, restrict exports, or limit the Chinese presence.
The length of the leases (49 years in Russia, 99 years in Zambia)
reduces this risk, but does not eliminate it. The difference with
Indonesia (2026) is that these States need Chinese investments to
modernize their land, which creates a mutual dependence that tempers the
temptation of a unilateral decree.

Massive Chinese investments could increase the differential rent of this
land: irrigation, fertilizers, infrastructure, improved seeds. They
would strengthen China's position in the \textbf{dialectic of controlled
solvency} (cf. §5.5.5) by anchoring activity in the host territories.
But even with these investments, the operation would not be transformed
into a rent extraction in the sense of the ToRE: it would remain a
productive investment in a weak externality, securing supply flows
without creating advance exogenous demand or polarized growth in China.

Legislative changes in the host countries — for example, allowing
foreigners to become owners of agricultural land — would not suffice
to transform these operations into rent extraction. These States would
retain their Sovereignty Rent, and foreign assets are not 'Spaces of
Value' frozen by a symbolic prohibition; they are fully integrated into
the world market, even if Western sanctions limit access to it.

**Synthesis: a niche accumulation, not a new rent-extraction cycle**

The China-Russia association, whether in agricultural land or energy joint ventures (86 projects, 222 billion dollars, key sectors), is a **strategic partnership between sovereign States**, not a rent-extraction cycle. The same applies to all Chinese agricultural investments in Africa, Latin America and Southeast Asia. These operations secure physical flows (energy, food) and create shared rents, but they do not resolve Chinese Stasis.

The foreign land leased or exploited by Chinese interests is an example of **niche accumulation** — a strategy for circumventing the domestic land constraint which, without creating a polarized growth cycle, contributes to the resilience of the Chinese productive apparatus. This niche accumulation is a pragmatic response to the exhaustion of the domestic stock of Value, but it does not constitute a new pioneer front capable of generating the advance exogenous demand necessary to restart the rent-extraction cycle in China.

#### 5.5.5. The port Hardened Enclaves: a response to the constraints of sovereignty

Given the vulnerability of processing investments (HPAL plants) to the Sovereignty Rent of host States, China has developed an alternative: **port Hardened Enclaves**. The port of Chancay in Peru, inaugurated in November 2024, is its archetype. Unlike the HPAL plants, Chancay is a pure extraction infrastructure: a mineral port designed to export South American copper, lithium and iron ore to China, without any local processing capacity.

Chinese loan contracts include structural conditions that, without being political conditionalities in the classical sense, constrain the sovereign room for manoeuvre of the host State. Thus, at Chancay: exclusive operating rights granted to COSCO, regulatory exemptions obtained by legislative means, and total collateral (all-assets pledge) secured against the entirety of the project's assets. This architecture renders any unilateral modification of the rules by the host State economically destructive.

The "dialectic of controlled solvency"\footnote{The notion of a "dialectic of controlled solvency" is an interpretation by the author. It aims to formalize a tension observed between two objectives of Chinese foreign policy — maintaining solvent partners in order to preserve the outlets and incomes of investments, while managing the risks of devaluation linked to the Sovereignty Rent. It does not correspond to any official Chinese doctrine, and is not formulated as such in institutional documents or public declarations. This interpretation is proposed as a reading hypothesis, not as a description of Beijing's intentional strategy.} that underlies this strategy rests on the idea that the host State is kept afloat — just enough to service the debt and buy Chinese goods — but not enough to develop an autonomous industry or free itself from dependence. China does not wish to make its partners totally insolvent (for they would cease to be outlets), nor to make them fully solvent (for they would free themselves from its dependence). The objective is a precarious equilibrium, calibrated by contractual clauses, collateral and regulatory exemptions.

Chancay illustrates the temporal duality of Hardened Enclaves: a defensive transition phase (geopolitical turnstile) that mutates into an offensive stationary phase (automated robotic node). This model generalizes to all strategic ports financed by the Silk Roads: Djibouti, Gwadar, Piraeus, Hambantota. China renounces industrial processing in order to concentrate on securing physical flows.

#### 5.5.6. The accounting role of the immaterial bubble

The bubble of AI tokens and carbon quotas (cf. Part III) plays an accounting role in this mechanism. It makes it possible to nominally revalue the collateral of Chinese loans (the operating rights over foreign assets) without this revaluation corresponding to an increase in the physical value of the assets. The destruction of material Wealth is thus partially "absorbed" by the inflation of Chinese immaterial assets. But this mechanism has its limits: it cannot indefinitely compensate for massive real losses, as the Venezuelan experience shows.

**Concluding remark:** This externalization mechanism is not a strategy of domination but a **structural response to the exhaustion of the Chinese material cycle**. China, like any State having reached the nodal phase, must manage the destruction of its material Wealth. The Chinese specificity is to have attempted to relocate part of this destruction towards the host States of its external investments. This attempt has had partial successes (port enclaves) and costly failures (Indonesia, Venezuela). The overhaul of Chinese lending instruments abroad — notably through the generalization of Hardened Enclaves — aims to stabilize this mechanism and to reduce the risks of conflict linked to the Sovereignty Rent, without ever eliminating them completely. China is learning, through crises, that structural asymmetry does not confer absolute immunity on it, and that the management of the periphery requires a fine dosage between the securing of flows and the acceptance of occasional losses.
