### T.3. Dynamic fragility

#### T.3.1. The bubble paradox

The calculation of $\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}}$ (T.3.5) gives $\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}}(A_{\text{eco}}, A_{\text{geo}}) = 0.796$, which classifies the pair $(A_{\text{eco}}, A_{\text{geo}})$ (extreme polarised growth × hyper-concentrated metropolis) in the category "structurally coherent".

However, $(A_{\text{eco}}, A_{\text{geo}})$ is a speculative bubble. How can such a fragile state be qualified as coherent?

\textbf{Answer.} The paradox comes from a confusion between \textbf{coherence} and \textbf{viability}. $\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}}$ measures the structural coherence (topological compatibility), not the economic durability. A bubble is structurally coherent (it forms a deep well, difficult to leave by the sole internal dynamics) but economically ephemeral (it is sensitive to external shocks).

\textbf{Physical analogy: supercooling.} Water can remain liquid below 0°C if it is pure and undisturbed. It is a structurally coherent but energetically unfavourable state. A simple perturbation suffices to trigger the brutal transition towards the solid state.

#### T.3.2. The spectral gap

\textbf{Definition T.3.1 (Spectral gap).} For an attractor $A_{\text{eco}}$:

$$\mathrm{gap}(A) = \min\{|\lambda_k(A)| > 0\}$$

The spectral gap measures the robustness margin of the potential well: a wide gap means that the well is robust; a narrow gap means that a small shock can make it tip.

\textbf{Physical analogy.} The spectral gap is the analogue of the HOMO--LUMO gap in quantum chemistry: a large gap means a stable molecule (little reactive), a small gap means an unstable molecule (very reactive).

#### T.3.3. The dynamic fragility index $\mathcal{F}$

\textbf{Definition T.3.2 (Dynamic fragility).} For an attractor $A_{\text{eco}}$:

$$\boxed{\mathcal{F}(A) = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{gap}(A)}{\mathrm{gap}_{\max}}}$$

where $\mathrm{gap}_{\max} = 0.50$ is the maximal gap observed in the model.

$\mathcal{F} \in [0,1]$: $\mathcal{F} \approx 0$ = robust system; $\mathcal{F} \approx 1$ = fragile system.

For a pair $(A_{\text{eco}}, A_{\text{geo}})$:

$$\mathcal{F}(A_{\text{eco}}, A_{\text{geo}}) = \max\big(\mathcal{F}(A_{\text{eco}}), \mathcal{F}(A_{\text{geo}})\big)$$

The maximum rule expresses that the pair breaks at its weakest link.

#### T.3.4. The viability index $\mathcal{S}$

\textbf{Definition T.3.3 (Viability).}

$$\boxed{\mathcal{S}(A,B) = \mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}}(A,B) \cdot (1 - \mathcal{F}(A,B))}$$

\textbf{Standard qualification} (Appendix X):

- \textbf{Viable} if $\mathcal{S} > 0.15$;
- \textbf{Fragile} if $0.05 < \mathcal{S} \leq 0.15$;
- \textbf{Ephemeral} if $\mathcal{S} \leq 0.05$.

\textbf{Particular cases} (Appendix X, §X.2):

- \textbf{Forbidden}: violation of the nilpotency $(g\cdot x)^2 = 0$ (6 pairs);
- \textbf{Terminal}: absorbing well $(T_{\text{eco}}, T_{\text{geo}})$ (1 pair);
- \textbf{Bubble}: $3P \times 3G$ (9 pairs).

> \textbf{The central message.} The distinction between $\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}}$ and $\mathcal{S}$ is fundamental for steering. A decision-maker who only looks at coherence risks maintaining a bubble believing it is stable. A decision-maker who looks at viability sees the fragility and can anticipate the bursting.

#### T.3.5. The general formula of borromean cohesion

\textbf{Question treated.} \textit{What makes a pair of attractors constitute a deep potential well, rather than a simple coexistence of two compatible structures?}

\textbf{Answer.} This depth is not an additive property. It depends on the way the two attractors articulate \textit{in the graph}, not on what they are in isolation. This is the meaning of the qualifier \textit{borromean}: the cohesion resides in the interlacing, not in the components.

\textbf{Two distinct structures.} It is important not to confuse:

- The \textbf{dual graph of the Merkabah} (T.1.1--T.1.3): 66 pairs, of which 55 adjacent and 11 non-adjacent. Connected, of diameter 2.
- The \textbf{strict hierarchical graph} on the 20 attractors: constructed in \textbf{Appendix Z, §Z.3}, analysed in Z.4. It is \textit{in this graph} that the distance $d_{\text{topo}}$ intervening in the formula is measured.

> \textbf{Point of vigilance.} The diameter 2 of the dual graph of the Merkabah is \textit{not} the diameter of the hierarchical graph of the 20 attractors. Confusing the two leads to incorrectly normalising the topological friction.

\textbf{The three factors.}

1. The \textbf{combined polarity} -- structural factor, carried by $\mathcal{B}_0$.
2. The \textbf{topological distance} -- friction factor, carried by $d_{\text{topo}}$.
3. The \textbf{hierarchical position} -- modulation factor, carried by the bonus term $h$.

\textbf{Definition T.3.4 (Borromean cohesion -- unique definition).} For two attractors $A_{\text{eco}}$ and $B_{\text{eco}}$:

$$\boxed{\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}}(A,B) = \underbrace{\mathcal{B}_0(A,B)}_{\text{structural}} \;-\; \underbrace{\alpha\, d_{\text{topo}}(A,B)}_{\text{friction}} \;+\; \underbrace{\beta_1\, \mathbb{1}_{\text{same level}} + \beta_2\, \mathbb{1}_{\text{same community}}}_{\text{hierarchical modulation}}}$$

with:
- $\mathcal{B}_0(A,B)$ defined by the equation of T.2.3;
- $d_{\text{topo}}(A,B)$ the normalised distance in the strict hierarchical graph (Z.3--Z.4);
- $\alpha = 0.03$, $\beta_1 = 0.08$, $\beta_2 = 0.05$ (calibration in Z.5.4);
- $\mathbb{1}_{\text{same level}}$ and $\mathbb{1}_{\text{same community}}$ the membership indicators.

\textbf{Note.} The quantity $\mathcal{H}(A,B)\cdot\mathcal{B}_{\text{ext}}(T_A,T_B)$ defined in T.2.3 is the \textit{base potential} $\mathcal{B}_0$. It does \textbf{not} constitute the borromean cohesion: it is a term of the formula above, which must be corrected by the topological friction and the hierarchical modulation.

\textbf{Structural properties.}

1. \textbf{Symmetry.} $\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}}(A,B) = \mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}}(B,A)$.
2. \textbf{Monotonicity.} $\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}}$ is increasing in each of its arguments at fixed polarity and position.
3. \textbf{Boundedness.} The calibration satisfies $\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}} \in [0,1]$ on the 400 pairs (control in Z.6).
4. \textbf{Degenerate case.} When $d_{\text{topo}}(A,B) = 0$ and $h(A,B) = 0$, the formula reduces to $\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}} = \mathcal{B}_0$.

Point 4 is the \textit{only} place where the harmonic construction reappears as a result. It is not a second definition: it is a consequence of the first, in a particular case.

\textbf{Forbidden pairs.} The six pairs excluded by the nilpotency are so \textit{before} the application of the general formula. They are not pairs whose cohesion would be weak: they are pairs which do not belong to the space of accessible states.

> \textbf{Note on counterfactual values.} When values are displayed for such pairs (cf. Z.6.1), they are \textbf{counterfactual}: they give what the formula would produce if the nilpotency constraint were lifted. They describe no real state.

The choice between the two is a question of \textbf{structural preference} (coherence vs robustness), not of absolute superiority.

##### T.4.2.1. The Chinese Stasis $(S_{\text{eco}}, S_{\text{geo}})$

The pair is structurally little coherent ($\mathcal{B}_0 = 0.116$) and dynamically very fragile ($\mathcal{F} = 0.82$). It is a state of \textbf{double fragility}: the well is little deep \textit{and} its col is close.

\textbf{TRR prescription.} Aim at a pair $(D_{\text{eco}}, D_{\text{geo}})$ or $(F_{\text{eco}}, F_{\text{geo}})$, that is to say a state whose viability exceeds $\mathcal{S} = 0.226$ (that is a factor \textbf{~5} compared to 0.044). The TRR is not a marginal improvement of the occupied well: it constitutes a \textbf{change of basin}.

##### T.4.2.2. The maximal bubble $(A_{\text{eco}}, A_{\text{geo}})$

The bubble is structurally coherent ($\mathcal{B}_0 = 0.666$, $\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}} = 0.796$) but dynamically ephemeral ($\mathcal{F} = 0.90$). It is this duality which makes it dangerous: it \textit{seems} stable as long as one only looks at the coherence. Its viability ($\mathcal{S} = 0.080$) classifies it in \textbf{Fragile} ($0.05 < \mathcal{S} \leq 0.15$), which means that it can last a few years, but not durably.

\textbf{Note}: the 9 bubbles have $\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}}$ comprised between \textbf{0.629 and 0.799}. The 3 diagonal cases ($(A_{\text{eco}}, A_{\text{geo}})$, $(B_{\text{eco}}, B_{\text{geo}})$, $(C_{\text{eco}}, C_{\text{geo}})$) are the highest (0.782--0.799); the 6 crossed pairs are lower (0.629--0.681). All remain $> 0.60$.

##### T.4.2.3. The growth optimum $(F_{\text{eco}}, F_{\text{geo}})$

The pair $(F_{\text{eco}}, F_{\text{geo}})$ combines a moderate structural coherence ($\mathcal{B}_0 = 0.343$, $\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}} = 0.473$) and a high dynamic robustness ($\mathcal{F} = 0.52$). It is the most durable state of the model: tempered growth does not require maximal cohesion, it requires maximal \textbf{viability}.

\textbf{Alternative optimum.} The pair $(D_{\text{eco}}, D_{\text{geo}})$ reaches a quasi-identical viability ($\mathcal{S} = 0.226$), with a slightly lower coherence (0.452) but a lower fragility (0.50). Both are \textbf{optima}; the choice depends on the preference between coherence and robustness.

##### T.4.2.4. The paradoxical collapse $(T_{\text{eco}}, T_{\text{geo}})$

The pair $(T_{\text{eco}}, T_{\text{geo}})$ presents a high structural coherence ($\mathcal{B}_0 = 0.502$, $\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}} = 0.632$) and an extreme fragility ($\mathcal{F} = 0.94$). It is the \textbf{paradoxical stability of collapse}: the system rests in a well attuned to itself, but this well is a state of death. Its viability is very low ($\mathcal{S} = 0.038$), which confirms that the collapse, although structurally coherent, is \textbf{economically untenable}.

\textbf{Particular status.} Contrary to the 6 strictly forbidden states (which violate the nilpotency), $(T_{\text{eco}}, T_{\text{geo}})$ is \textbf{topologically possible}. It is a \textbf{terminal state} (absorbing well), not a forbidden state. The distinction is important: a forbidden state cannot exist; a terminal state can exist, but one does not leave it without massive exogenous intervention (TRR).

#### T.4.3. The five results

1. Viability is \textbf{rare}: \textbf{2.75\%} of the pairs (11 out of 400).
2. Bubbles are \textbf{coherent but ephemeral} (high $\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}}$, low $\mathcal{S}$).
3. Stasis is a state of \textbf{double fragility} (low $\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}}$, high $\mathcal{F}$).
4. The optimum is \textbf{tempered growth} $(2P+1N \times 2G+1H)$, with two variants: $(F_{\text{eco}}, F_{\text{geo}})$ and $(D_{\text{eco}}, D_{\text{geo}})$.
5. The TRR is a \textbf{basin jump} (factor ~5 of viability: 0.044 → 0.226).

### T.5. Empirical validation

#### T.5.1. Method and criteria

For each historical case: 

(1) determine the binary configurations $\mathbf{x}_{\text{eco}}$ and $\mathbf{y}_{\text{geo}}$;
(2) identify the dominant attractors $A_{\text{eco}}$ and $A_{\text{geo}}$ (Appendix M);
(3) calculate $\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}}$, $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{S}$; (4) confront the diagnosis with the historiography; (5) validate or invalidate.

\textbf{Validation criteria.}

- \textbf{Strong validation:} the diagnosis $\mathcal{S}$ is coherent with the observed durability \textit{and} the transitions respect the spectral thresholds.
- \textbf{Weak validation:} the diagnosis is compatible with the observed durability, but requires an \textit{ad hoc} interpretation (for example, "ephemeral" meaning "structurally non-durable" and not "imminent collapse").
- \textbf{Falsifying:} a state predicted "ephemeral" has lasted more than 30 years without collapse; a state predicted "viable" has collapsed in less than 5 years; a transition has violated the rule of polar thresholds.

The qualitative diagnosis (Viable / Fragile / Ephemeral) is more robust than the exact numerical value. The Great Depression is \textbf{Ephemeral} (in the sense of the classification by $\mathcal{S}$), and not "Forbidden" (which is a combinatorial category reserved for violations of nilpotency).

\textbf{Honest reading.} Out of 8 cases:

- \textbf{4 strong validations} (Trente Glorieuses, China 1978--2018, Great Depression, Chinese Republic);
- \textbf{1 weak validation} (post-2018 China, exit not yet observed);
- \textbf{3 very weak validations} (Japan, Qing, Southern Song): the diagnosis "ephemeral" is \textit{compatible} with a long duration only if one admits that "ephemeral" means "structurally non-durable" and not "imminent collapse". This is an \textbf{ad hoc interpretation} which weakens the predictive scope.

\textbf{Absence of falsifying case.} No case of the corpus falsifies the model. But the corpus has been \textbf{selected after the fact} on the basis of the diagnosis. A prospective validation protocol (predict \textit{before} observing) remains to be constructed.

\textbf{Conclusion.} The validation is a \textbf{retrospective coherence}, not a validation in the strong predictive sense. This distinction is essential and must be recalled each time the word "validation" is used.

> \textbf{Synthesis of the validation.} The eight historical cases examined are compatible with the structural diagnosis of the model. This convergence constitutes a \textbf{validation of coherence}, not a validation in the strong predictive sense: the cases have been selected after the fact on the basis of the diagnosis. The precise epistemological status of this validation is specified in T.6.3.

### T.6. Epistemological foundation

#### T.6.1. The common ground

The \textbf{five} frameworks mobilised by the model are heterogeneous by their origin. It is important to distinguish them according to their \textbf{role} and their \textbf{founding author}.

\textbf{Frameworks describing the relational dynamics} (what the system \textit{does}):

1. \textbf{The Theory of Rent Extraction (ToRE)} -- historical model of stock and flows, developed by \textbf{Thierry Rebour}. It describes the conversion of frozen assets (Space of Value) into productive flows (Space of Wealth), and the resulting rent extraction cycles.

2. \textbf{The Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$} -- algebraic formalism of signatures and nilpotency, whose structure was developed by \textbf{Peter Rowlands} (2007). It is to Rowlands that one owes:
   - the definition of the \textbf{12 pentads} (6 positive $P_1$--$P_6$, 6 negative $N_1$--$N_6$) as irreducible composite units of $\mathrm{Cl}(6,0)$;
   - the \textbf{filtration $64 \to 20$} via the geometry of the \textbf{Merkabah} (level 3 double tetrahedron), which reduces the 64 configurations of $\mathrm{Cl}(6,0)$ to 20 stable attractors (the 20 vertices of the dual dodecahedron);
   - the \textbf{neighbourhood rule} by sharing of triangular face, which defines the partition into 20 equivalence classes.
   
   The $\mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$ formalism extends this framework to a space with 12 generators (6 economic + 6 geographic), but the combinatorial structure (pentads, filtration $64 \to 20$) remains that of Rowlands.

3. \textbf{Topological hydrodynamics} -- developed by \textbf{Mikhail I. Aksman} (2026). It describes the \textbf{vortons} (vorticity singularities) and the \textbf{DSM-861 network} (triangular network of 861 nodes emerging from turbulence on a torus). This framework provides the \textbf{physical substrate} which justifies the emergence of stable structures (the 20 attractors) from turbulence.

4. \textbf{Dense associative dynamics} -- developed by \textbf{Dmitry Krotov and John J. Hopfield} (2016). The central result mobilised is the following: by generalising the energy function of classical Hopfield networks (interaction of order $n$, $F(x) = x^n$), the storage capacity grows as $N^{n-1}$. \textbf{Order 3} ($n=3$) is optimal: it maximises the depth of the attraction wells while avoiding the fragility of higher orders. It is this result which justifies, in the $\mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$ model, the \textbf{triadic structure} of attractors (pentad triplets) and the \textbf{cubic depth} of potential wells (T.1.2).

\textbf{Framework providing the arithmetic support} (what makes the system \textit{computable}):

5. \textbf{The exceptional lattice $\Lambda_{72}$} -- constructed by \textbf{Gabriele Nebe} (2010). It is a pair unimodular lattice of dimension 72 and minimum 8, whose automorphism group contains $(\mathrm{PSL}_2(7) \times \mathrm{SL}_2(25)):2$. This lattice provides the \textbf{discrete spectrum} from which are extracted the \textbf{15 constants $\beta_k$} (square roots of 15 specific eigenvalues of the Gram matrix $G_{72}$).

\textbf{Why this distinction is essential.} The first four frameworks describe the \textbf{relational dynamics}: they say \textit{what} the system does (convert, transition, stabilise, emerge). The fifth framework provides the \textbf{arithmetic support}: it says \textit{with which numbers} the system does it. Without $\Lambda_{72}$ and the 15 $\beta_k$, the general formula of T.3.5 would remain \textbf{qualitative}; with them, it becomes \textbf{quantitative}.

\textbf{Attribution of structural contributions.} It is appropriate not to confuse:

- \textbf{Rowlands} provides the \textbf{combinatorial structure} (pentads, filtration $64 \to 20$, Merkabah);
- \textbf{Nebe} provides the \textbf{arithmetic support} (lattice $\Lambda_{72}$, 15 $\beta_k$);
- \textbf{Krotov--Hopfield} provides the \textbf{dynamic justification} of the triadic order (DAM);
- \textbf{Aksman} provides the \textbf{physical substrate} (vortons, DSM-861);
- \textbf{Rebour} provides the \textbf{economic framework} (ToRE).

The $\mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$ model is the \textbf{synthesis} of these five contributions: it does not replace them, it articulates them.

\textbf{Precision on "associative dynamics".} The term does not designate a generic theory, but the \textbf{Krotov--Hopfield corpus on Dense Associative Memories (DAM)}, published in 2016.

\textbf{The common ground.} What these five frameworks share -- and which justifies their bringing together -- is the following:

> \textbf{Common ground claimed by the model.} A system closed on a stock can only regenerate its Value by \textbf{converting one form into another}. The thresholds mark the configurations where this conversion becomes possible or impossible. The \textbf{spectral invariants} of $\Lambda_{72}$ provide the \textbf{numbers} which render this conversion computable, and the \textbf{filtration $64 \to 20$} of Rowlands provides the \textbf{structure} which constrains it.

In each framework, this idea takes a different vocabulary:

- \textbf{ToRE}: destruction and recreation of rent (conversion of frozen assets into productive flows);
- \textbf{$\mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$} (Rowlands): nilpotency and impossibility of return to the identical; the stable configurations are those which satisfy $(g\cdot x)^2 = 0$, and the filtration $64 \to 20$ selects the 20 attractors;
- \textbf{Hydrodynamics} (Aksman): reconnection of circulation and change of topology of the vortex; the stable structures emerge from turbulence;
- \textbf{Krotov--Hopfield}: recomposition of representations; the stored patterns are attraction wells of order 3;
- \textbf{$\Lambda_{72}$} (Nebe): the 15 $\beta_k$ are the \textbf{spectral invariants} which parameterise the conversion.

> \textbf{Status of this common ground.} This common ground is a \textbf{working hypothesis}, not a theorem. It explains why the bringing together is fruitful; it does not prove that the frameworks are equivalent.

#### T.6.2. The five validity criteria

A connection between two frameworks is judged on five criteria:

1. \textbf{Structural isomorphism.} Does there exist an explicit application preserving the relations, and not only a vocabulary analogy?
2. \textbf{Independence of sources.} Have the two frameworks been constructed without knowledge of each other?
3. \textbf{Joint prediction.} Does the bringing together produce a non-trivial prediction, formulable in both frameworks and testable?
4. \textbf{Robustness to parameterisation.} Does the correspondence survive a reasonable variation of the coefficients?
5. \textbf{Falsifiability.} What observation would allow invalidating it?

> \textbf{The decisive criterion: number 4.} It is this criterion which led to abandoning the old postulated lookup table and the friction $\Delta(T_E,T_G)$ adjusted to reproduce it. A calibration which inverts the direction of reasoning -- starting from the answer to manufacture the parameter -- produces no knowledge. The derivation of Z.5 is submitted to this criterion: the coefficients must be fixed \textit{before} the calculation of the 400 pairs, not after.

\textbf{Optimality of order 3} (Krotov--Hopfield)
  & \textbf{1, 4} & \textbf{Demonstrated} (T.1.2) \\
\hline
7 thresholds $\leftrightarrow$ 7 catastrophes of Thom
  & 1, 4 & \textbf{Partially founded} \\
\hline
$64 \to 20$ $\leftrightarrow$ Mandarin phonology
  & 1, 2, 4 & \textbf{Partially founded} \\
\hline
$64 \to 20$ $\leftrightarrow$ Tang alliances
  & 1, 2, 4 & \textbf{Partially founded} \\
\hline
ToRE $\leftrightarrow$ $\mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$
  & 1, 4 & \textbf{Partially founded} \\
\hline
\textbf{Selection of the 15 indices $I_{15}$}
  & \textbf{1 partial} & \textbf{Open research programme} \\
\hline
\textbf{Bijection bivectors $\leftrightarrow$ $\beta_k$}
  & \textbf{1} & \textbf{Strong conjecture (arbitrary assignment)} \\
\hline
$\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}} \leftrightarrow$ depth of wells
  & 1 & \textbf{Speculative} \\
\hline
$64 \to 20$ $\leftrightarrow$ genetic code
  & 2 & \textbf{Speculative} \\
\hline
Validation on 8 historical cases
  & 3 partial & \textbf{Retrospective coherence} \\
\hline
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

\textbf{Reading of the table.}

- \textbf{Demonstrated (internal):} the result is a property of the formalism. Its truth does not prejudge its adequacy to the real.
- \textbf{Partially founded:} the structure is correctly put in correspondence, but criteria 3 and 5 are not satisfied.
- \textbf{Open research programme:} the question is identified, the paths are traced, but no demonstration is provided.
- \textbf{Strong conjecture:} the coherence is real, but the assignment is arbitrary ($15!$ possible permutations).
- \textbf{Speculative:} only a counting isomorphism or an independence of source is established. These connections are preserved as \textit{heuristics}, never as proofs.
- \textbf{Retrospective coherence:} the validation shows that the model does not contradict the examined cases. It does not show that it would have predicted them.

#### T.6.4. What the model does not claim to do

1. \textbf{No mystical proof.} The mobilised traditions (\textit{Yi Jing}, \textit{wuxing}, Tang kinship) are treated as empirical qualitative modelisations of cyclical dynamics, not as revelations.
2. \textbf{No literal physical identification.} The economy is not a fluid. Vortons and octahedra are structural analogues.
3. \textbf{No calendrical forecast.} Thresholds characterise regimes, not dates.
4. \textbf{No validation by the number of analogies.} Accumulating correspondences does not reinforce their validity: if they derive from the same underlying structure, they only count for one.
5. \textbf{No confusion between "forbidden" and "terminal".} The 6 strictly forbidden states (violation of the nilpotency) are \textbf{topologically impossible}. The terminal state $(T_{\text{eco}}, T_{\text{geo}})$ is \textbf{topologically possible} but \textbf{economically dead}. The distinction is essential: it separates the impossible from the simply undesirable.
6. \textbf{No reduction of $\Lambda_{72}$ to a simple calculation tool.} Nebe's lattice is not a "reservoir of constants" that one could replace by any other spectrum. Its arithmetic structure (unimodular, pair, minimum 8, exceptional automorphism group) is \textbf{necessary} for the 15 $\beta_k$ to produce the bijection $64 \to 64$ and the binomial distribution $C(6,k)$ (Chapter 15). Another lattice would give other constants, and \textbf{would break} the coherence of the model.
7. \textbf{No reduction of Krotov--Hopfield to a simple analogy.} The optimality of order 3 is not a metaphor: it is a \textbf{theorem} on the capacity of dense associative networks. It justifies \textit{a priori} the triadic structure of attractors, independently of any economic consideration.

\section*{Appendix W -- The traditional Chinese grids}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Appendix W -- The traditional Chinese grids}

\subsection*{W.1. The Chinese rhyme tables (\textnormal{韵图}, \textit{yuntu})}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{W.1. The Chinese rhyme tables}

The Chinese phonological tradition produced, as early as the end of the Tang period (9\textsuperscript{th}--10\textsuperscript{th} century), systems of syllable classification of remarkable rigour. These \textbf{rhyme tables} (\textnormal{韵图}, \textit{yuntu}) constitute the oldest and most documented manifestation of the $64 \to 20$ invariant in the linguistic domain. The oldest complete \textnormal{韵图} preserved is the \textnormal{《韵镜》} (\textit{Yunjing}), whose \textnormal{底本} (original text) dates from the Tang, even if the preserved version is a reprint from the Southern Song.

\paragraph{W.1.1. The \textit{Qieyun} (\textnormal{切韵}, 601) and the \textit{Guangyun} (\textnormal{广韵}, 1008).}

The \textit{Qieyun}, compiled by Lu Fayan (\textnormal{陆法言}) in 601, is the first Chinese rhyme dictionary to propose a systematic classification of syllables. It distinguishes:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{193 rhymes} (\textnormal{韵}, \textit{yùn}), grouped according to their vocalic final.
    \item \textbf{4 tones} (\textnormal{四声}, \textit{sìshēng}): \textnormal{平} (\textit{píng}, level), \textnormal{上} (\textit{shǎng}, rising), \textnormal{去} (\textit{qù}, departing), \textnormal{入} (\textit{rù}, entering).
    \item \textbf{$\sim$21 initials} (\textnormal{声母}, \textit{shēngmǔ}), classified according to their point of articulation.
\end{itemize}

The \textit{Guangyun}, an augmented version of the \textit{Qieyun} published under the Song dynasty in 1008, brings the number of rhymes to \textbf{206}.

\paragraph{W.1.2. The combinatorial structure.}

The Cartesian product of the three phonological dimensions gives the space of possible syllables:

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Combinatorial structure of classical Chinese phonology (\textit{Guangyun})}
\label{tab:W1_structure_phonologique_classique}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{|>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{4cm}|>{\centering\arraybackslash}p{2cm}|>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X|}
\hline
\textbf{Dimension} & \textbf{Number} & \textbf{Nature} \\
\hline
Initials (\textnormal{声母}) & $\sim 21$ & Attack consonants, classified by point of articulation (\textnormal{唇}/\textnormal{齿}/\textnormal{舌}/\textnormal{牙}/\textnormal{喉}) \\
\hline
Rhymes/Finals (\textnormal{韵}) & 206 & Vowels + codas, classified by quality and length \\
\hline
Tones (\textnormal{声调}) & 4 & Height and melodic contour (\textnormal{平上去入}) \\
\hline
\textbf{Total space} & $\sim 21 \times 206 \times 4 \approx 17\,304$ & Theoretical combinations \\
\hline
\textbf{Attested syllables} & $\sim 3\,700$ & Combinations effectively realised in the language \\
\hline
\textbf{Gaps} & $\sim 13\,600$ & Combinations forbidden by phonotactic constraints \\
\hline
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

\paragraph{W.1.3. The reduction towards 20 classes: the $64 \to 20$ invariant.}

In modern Mandarin phonology, the simplification of the system leads to:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\sim 21$ initials (unchanged)
    \item $\sim 35$ finals (drastic reduction of the 206 rhymes of the \textit{Guangyun})
    \item 4 tones (the \textit{rù} tone has disappeared in standard Mandarin, redistributed among the other three)
\end{itemize}

The product $21 \times 35 \times 4 \approx 2\,940$ theoretical combinations is reduced to about \textbf{400 distinct syllables} in modern Mandarin. Among these, structural analysis reveals the existence of \textbf{20 fundamental phonological classes}, isomorphic to the 20 attractors of the economic model.

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=blue!5!white,colframe=blue!75!black,title=$64 \to 20$ invariant in Mandarin phonology]
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Input}: 64 basic syllabic combinations (initials $\times$ finals $\times$ tones, after filtration of redundancies).
    \item \textbf{Output}: 20 stable phonological classes.
    \item \textbf{Filtration mechanism}: articulatory constraints (phonetic impossibility) and distributional constraints (phonotactic gaps).
    \item \textbf{Fill rate}: $\sim 65\,\%$ (26 active cases out of 40 in the 5×8 grid).
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Admissible bounds and exact number.} The $64 \to 20$ reduction in Mandarin phonology does not mean that the system produces exactly 20 classes by topological constraint. The geometry of the Merkabah fixes the \textbf{admissible bounds} (the 20 possible classes, the 5 phases of the \textit{wuxing}, the 4 polarity signatures); the phonological system populates the \textbf{coordinates} according to its articulatory constraints and its evolutionary history. The exact number of realised classes (20 in standard Mandarin) is an empirical fact, not a topological necessity. This distinction is the same as that which separates, in biology, the architecture of the genetic code (20 possible amino acids) from the effective number of codons per amino acid (1 to 6 depending on the amino acid).

\paragraph{W.1.4. Phonotactic gaps: the linguistic equivalent of frustrated configurations.}

Just as the economic model rejects 24 configurations (violation of nilpotency, cf. Appendix Y), Mandarin phonology presents \textbf{phonotactic gaps}: combinations which violate no explicit rule but which are structurally impossible to pronounce or which do not exist in the system.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Examples of phonotactic gaps in Mandarin}
\label{tab:W1_lacunes_phonotactiques}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{|>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3cm}|>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3cm}|>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X|}
\hline
\textbf{Combination} & \textbf{Status} & \textbf{Reason} \\
\hline
\textit{tl-} in initial position & Forbidden & Articulatory constraint: impossible to pronounce in Mandarin \\
\hline
\textit{-ng} in final position followed by \textit{-p/-t/-k} & Forbidden & Coda constraint: incompatibility of nasal and occlusive codas \\
\hline
Syllable without initial nor final & Forbidden & Structural constraint: every syllable must have at least one vowel \\
\hline
\textit{rù} tone in standard Mandarin & Disappeared & Historical evolution: redistribution towards the three other tones \\
\hline
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

These gaps are the \textbf{signature of deep structural constraints}, analogous to the frustrated configurations of the economic model. The distinction between \textbf{structural} gaps (universal, linked to nilpotency) and \textbf{conjunctural} gaps (historical, linked to the evolution of the system) is analysed in §25.5.2.

\subsection*{W.2. The other traditional Chinese grids}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{W.2. The other traditional Chinese grids}

Chinese correlative thought has produced numerous other classification grids, all structured according to similar principles of combination and filtration.

\paragraph{W.2.1. The 10 heavenly stems (\textnormal{天干}, \textit{tiāngān}) and the 12 earthly branches (\textnormal{地支}, \textit{dìzhī}).}

The Chinese sexagesimal cycle combines 10 heavenly stems and 12 earthly branches to form 60 unique combinations (and not $10 \times 12 = 120$, because only combinations of the same parity are permitted).

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{The sexagesimal cycle: 10 stems × 12 branches → 60 combinations}
\label{tab:W2_cycle_sexagesimal}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{|>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3cm}|>{\centering\arraybackslash}p{2cm}|>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X|}
\hline
\textbf{Dimension} & \textbf{Number} & \textbf{Elements} \\
\hline
Heavenly stems (\textnormal{天干}) & 10 & \textnormal{甲乙丙丁戊己庚辛壬癸} (associated with the 5 \textit{wuxing} elements, in Yin/Yang versions) \\
\hline
Earthly branches (\textnormal{地支}) & 12 & \textnormal{子丑寅卯辰巳午未申酉戌亥} (associated with the 12 animals of the zodiac) \\
\hline
\textbf{Possible combinations} & $10 \times 12 = 120$ & Theoretical space \\
\hline
\textbf{Effective combinations} & \textbf{60} & Filtration by parity (Yin/Yang) \\
\hline
\textbf{Gaps} & \textbf{60} & Combinations forbidden by the parity rule \\
\hline
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

\textbf{A different invariant.} The sexagesimal cycle does not fall under the $64 \to 20$ invariant: it operates a $120 \to 60$ reduction (filtration by Yin/Yang parity), which is an invariant of a different structure. It is mentioned here to illustrate the generality of filtration mechanisms in Chinese correlative thought, not to be counted as an additional manifestation of the $64 \to 20$ invariant. This distinction is essential so as not to artificially inflate the number of independent confirmations.

\paragraph{W.2.2. The 28 lunar mansions (\textnormal{二十八宿}, \textit{èrshíbā xiù}).}

Traditional Chinese astronomy divides the sky into 28 lunar mansions, distributed in 4 groups of 7 (the 4 celestial palaces):

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{The 28 lunar mansions and the 4 celestial palaces}
\label{tab:W2_28_constellations}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{|>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3cm}|>{\centering\arraybackslash}p{2cm}|>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3cm}|>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X|}
\hline
\textbf{Palace} & \textbf{Number} & \textbf{Direction} & \textbf{Symbolic animal} \\
\hline
Azure Dragon (\textnormal{青龍}) & 7 & East & Dragon \\
\hline
Vermillion Bird (\textnormal{朱雀}) & 7 & South & Phoenix \\
\hline
White Tiger (\textnormal{白虎}) & 7 & West & Tiger \\
\hline
Black Warrior (\textnormal{玄武}) & 7 & North & Turtle-serpent \\

\textbf{Total} & \textbf{28} & 4 directions & 4 symbolic animals \\
\hline
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

The $4 \times 7 = 28$ structure is not arbitrary: it corresponds to the average lunar cycle ($\sim 27{,}3$ days). The 4 palaces are isomorphic to the 4 blocks of the tensor product (I, II, III, IV) of the $\mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$ model, and the 7 mansions of each palace are isomorphic to the 7 spectral thresholds ($S_1$ to $S_7$). This is not a manifestation of the $64 \to 20$ invariant, but a \textbf{different invariant} ($4 \times 7$), mentioned for its heuristic value.

\paragraph{W.2.3. The \textit{Luoshu} (\textnormal{洛书}) and the \textit{Hetu} (\textnormal{河图}): magic squares.}

The \textit{Luoshu} is a 3×3 magic square where the sum of each row, column, and diagonal equals 15:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
4 & 9 & 2 \\
\hline
3 & 5 & 7 \\
\hline
8 & 1 & 6 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

This square codes the distribution of the 9 numbers (1 to 9) according to a structure where the centre (5) plays a pivotal role, analogous to the \textbf{Earth} phase in the \textit{wuxing}. The 8 peripheral positions correspond to the 8 trigrams of the Bagua. This is not a manifestation of the $64 \to 20$ invariant, but a \textbf{historical formalisation} of the \textit{wuxing} and the Bagua, mentioned for its heuristic value.

\subsection*{W.3. Statistical validation of the 5×8 grid}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{W.3. Statistical validation of the 5×8 grid}

The validity of the 5×8 grid as a universal filtration structure can be tested statistically. We present here three complementary tests.

\paragraph{W.3.1. Spearman test: distribution of polarities.}

\textbf{Hypothesis:} the distribution of polarities observed in the four documented domains (physics, biology, phonology, Tang alliances) follows the theoretical gradient $(3, 5, 11, 1)$ (i.e., 3 attractors 3P, 5 attractors 2P+1N, 11 attractors 1P+2N, 1 attractor 3N).

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Spearman test: distribution of polarities}
\label{tab:W3_spearman_polarites}
\small
\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
\textbf{Domain} & \textbf{3P/+3} & \textbf{2P+1N/+2} & \textbf{1P+2N/+1} & \textbf{3N/−3} & \textbf{Correlation $\rho$} \\
\hline
Theoretical & 3 & 5 & 11 & 1 & — \\
\hline
Physics & 3 & 5 & 11 & 1 & $\rho = 1{,}000$ \\
\hline
Biology & 3 & 5 & 11 & 1 & $\rho = 1{,}000$ \\
\hline
Phonology & 3 & 5 & 11 & 1 & $\rho = 1{,}000$ \\
\hline
Tang alliances & 3 & 5 & 11 & 1 & $\rho = 1{,}000$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\textbf{Result:} the Spearman correlation is \textbf{perfect} ($\rho = 1{,}000$) in the four documented domains. The distribution of polarities follows exactly the theoretical gradient.

\paragraph{W.3.2. $\chi^2$ test: rejection of uniformity.}

The $\chi^2$ test compares the observed counts of polarity classes with the expected counts under the null hypothesis (uniform distribution). The result indicates a highly significant deviation ($p < 0{,}001$), confirming that the distribution of attractors is not random but structured by topological constraints.

\paragraph{W.3.3. Permutation test: rejection of chance.}

The permutation test evaluates the significance of the observed correlation by comparing it to the distribution of correlations obtained on 1,000 random correspondences. A p-value $< 0{,}01$ confirms that the observed correlation cannot be attributed to chance.

\textbf{Conclusion of the three tests:} the conjunction of Spearman ($\rho = 1{,}0$), $\chi^2$ (rejection of uniformity), and permutation (rejection of chance) constitutes a robust statistical validation of the hypothesis: the 5×8 grid is a filtration structure. This validation bears on the \textbf{four documented domains}; it does not prejudge the validity in the proposed domains (economics, geography), which remain to be tested by the same methods.

Some fall under the $64 \to 20$ invariant (rhyme tables, \textit{Yi Jing}, \textit{wuxing}, Bagua); others follow different invariants (sexagesimal cycle: $120 \to 60$). The $\mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$ model provides the mathematical formalism which unifies the former and distinguishes the latter. The convergence with particle physics, molecular biology, and political economy is \textbf{documented} for physics, biology, phonology, and Tang alliances; it is \textbf{proposed} for economics and geography.
\end{tcolorbox}

## Appendix X -- Combinatorial classification of the 400 pairs of attractors

### X.0. Object and positioning

#### X.0.1. Object of Appendix X

Appendix X presents the \textbf{combinatorial classification} of the 400 pairs of joint attractors $\mathcal{A}_{\text{eco}} \times \mathcal{A}_{\text{geo}}$. It defines:

- the \textbf{16 classes of combined polarity} ($3P \times 3G$, $3P \times 2G+1H$, ..., $3N \times 3H$);
- the \textbf{6 strictly forbidden states} (violation of nilpotency);
- \textbf{1 terminal state} $(T_{\text{eco}}, T_{\text{geo}})$ (absorbing well);
- the \textbf{9 bubble states} ($3P \times 3G$, metastable);
- the \textbf{384 stable or tense states}.

This classification relies exclusively on the \textbf{polarity of the pentad triplets} and on the nilpotency condition $(g \cdot x)^2 = 0$. It does not involve topological distance, nor stability indices.

#### X.0.2. What this appendix does not contain

In accordance with the non-redundancy principle (Appendix A, §A.0), Appendix X \textbf{does not contain}:

- the numerical values of $\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}}$, $\mathcal{F}$, $\mathcal{S}$;
- the qualifications Viable / Fragile / Ephemeral;
- the numbered catalogue of the 400 pairs.

These objects belong to \textbf{Appendix Z} (topological derivation) and \textbf{Appendix T} (interpretation).

### X.2. Unstable, forbidden, and paradoxical joint attractors

Although the space of geo-economic states is mathematically defined by the Cartesian product $\mathcal{A}_{\text{eco}} \times \mathcal{A}_{\text{geo}}$ (i.e., 400 pairs), the nilpotency condition $(g \cdot x)^2 = 0$ and the constraints of topological compatibility filter a part of these states.

## Appendix Y -- The logic of octahedra and the frustration of Group B

### Y.0. Object, epistemic status, and plan

#### Y.0.1. Object

This appendix resolves a problem left open in the main text:

> \textbf{Why are the configurations 011, 110, and 111 of Group B frustrated, while 000, 001, 010, 100, and 101 are valid?}

In the main text, this rule is stated in combinatorial form:

$$
\begin{cases}
\text{(R1)} & b_3 + b_4 + b_5 \leq 2 \\[6pt]
\text{(R2)} & b_3 = 0 \Longrightarrow b_4 + b_5 \leq 1 \\[6pt]
\text{(R3)} & b_5 = 0 \Longrightarrow b_3 + b_4 \leq 1
\end{cases}
$$

But this rule is not a \textbf{demonstration}. The object of this appendix is to \textbf{motivate} it on the geometric structure of the Merkabah, relying on the works of Hill \& Rowlands [@Hill_Rowlands_2007].

### Y.1. The structure of octahedra in the Merkabah

#### Y.1.1. The level 2 tetrahedron and the level 3 Merkabah

Hill \& Rowlands [@Hill_Rowlands_2007, §5] describe the structure of nested tetrahedra:

> "The tetrahedron of the 2nd level is composed of \textbf{1 octahedron and 4 tetrahedra} and at the third level, it is composed of \textbf{4 octahedra and 10 tetrahedra}."

The double tetrahedron (= Merkabah) doubles these values:

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Counts of octahedra, tetrahedra, codons and amino acids for orders 2 and 3.}
  \label{tab:octahedra-codons}
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lcccc@{}}
    \toprule
    Order & Octahedra & Tetrahedra & Codons & Amino acids \\
    \midrule
    2 & \textbf{2} & \textbf{8} & 16 & 8 \\
    3 & 8 & 20 & 64 & 20 \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\textbf{The level 3 Merkabah contains 8 octahedra and 20 tetrahedra.}

#### Y.1.2. The 8 octahedra and the 8 configurations of Group B

Group B is coded by 3 bits $(b_3, b_4, b_5)$, which gives $2^3 = 8$ configurations.

\textbf{Correspondence.} The 8 configurations of Group B are mapped bijectively onto the 8 octahedra of the level 3 Merkabah.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{cccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Code} & \textbf{Octahedron} & \textbf{Code} & \textbf{Octahedron} \\
\midrule
000 & $O_0$ & 100 & $O_4$ \\
001 & $O_1$ & 101 & $O_5$ \\
010 & $O_2$ & 110 & $O_6$ \\
011 & $O_3$ & 111 & $O_7$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

#### Y.1.3. Internal structure of an octahedron

Each octahedron has 8 triangular faces, 6 vertices, 12 edges. The 8 octahedra are located at the centre of the level 3 Merkabah, the 20 tetrahedra at the periphery. Each face of an octahedron is adjacent either to another octahedron, or to a peripheral tetrahedron.

\textbf{Definition Y.1 (polarity of a face).} In the level 3 Merkabah, each face of an octahedron is attached to a peripheral tetrahedron. The polarity of the face is defined by the orientation of the adjacent tetrahedron: tetrahedron pointing outwards (vertex directed away from the centre) $\to$ polarity $+$; tetrahedron pointing inwards $\to$ polarity $-$.

---

### Y.2. Geometric definition of the 3 bits and adjacencies

#### Y.2.1. The problem of the choice of the 3 regions

The octahedron possesses 3 principal axes of symmetry (North--South, East--West, High--Low) and 8 faces. To code a configuration by 3 bits, one must \textbf{group the 8 faces into 3 regions} and associate to each a bit of dominant polarity.

\textbf{Geometric attention.} A naive choice would consist in taking the 3 pairs of opposite faces (North/South, East/West, High/Low). But two opposite faces are not adjacent: they share no edge. The purity condition $b_3 b_4 = 0$ would then have no local topological justification.

#### Y.2.2. Conventional choice: three faces adjacent along a meridian

We adopt the following convention (figure Y.1, not reproduced here):

One chooses a vertex $S$ of the octahedron and \textbf{three faces} $F_3, F_4, F_5$ among the four faces incident to $S$. These three faces are arranged along a "meridian" of the octahedron, so that $F_3$ and $F_4$ share an edge issuing from $S$, $F_4$ and $F_5$ share an edge issuing from $S$, and $F_3$ and $F_5$ share no edge.

\textbf{Convention Y.1.} The 3 bits $(b_3, b_4, b_5)$ code the dominant polarity of the three faces $F_3, F_4, F_5$ thus chosen. The adjacent pairs are $(b_3, b_4)$ and $(b_4, b_5)$; the pair $(b_3, b_5)$ is non-adjacent.

\textbf{Remark.} This choice is a \textbf{projection convention}, not an absolute geometric necessity. It is motivated by the fact that it produces exactly the $8 \to 5$ filtration observed in the main text. A different choice (three adjacent pairs) would produce an $8 \to 4$ filtration, incompatible with the data (see Y.9.1).

#### Y.2.3. Polarity and parsimony

In the level 3 Merkabah, the peripheral tetrahedra are distributed into 8 tetrahedra of polarity $+$ (pointing outwards) and 12 tetrahedra of polarity $-$ (pointing inwards).

The polarity $+$ is therefore \textbf{minority} ($8/20 = 40\,\%$). This rarity is the fundamental physical fact which motivates axiom A1 below.

---

### Y.3. Axiom of polar parsimony and purity theorem

#### Y.3.1. Axiom A1 (polar parsimony)

\textbf{Axiom A1.} In the level 3 Merkabah, two adjacent faces of the same octahedron cannot simultaneously bear the polarity $+$.

\textbf{Justification -- and its circle.}

A1 is motivated by two considerations:

1. \textbf{The rarity of positive tetrahedra}: 8 tetrahedra $+$ out of 20 (40\%). A local co-activation of two adjacent $+$ would create a concentration incompatible with this rarity.
2. \textbf{Rowlands' polar closure condition}: the nilpotency $(g\cdot x)^2 = 0$ requires the cancellation of the bivectorial interaction terms.

\textbf{The circle.} Consideration (2) invokes the polar closure, which is precisely what the equivalence E1 (Y.5.3) postulates as equivalent to A1. There is therefore a \textbf{hermeneutic circle}: A1 justifies E1, and E1 justifies A1.

\textbf{How to exit the circle?} Two paths are open:

- \textbf{Demonstrative path} (not taken): derive A1 from the algebraic structure of $\mathrm{Cl}(6,0)$ without invoking the polar closure. This is a research programme.
- \textbf{Hermeneutic path} (taken): assume that A1 and E1 are \textbf{co-constituted} in a coherent reading of the Merkabah. The coherence of the system ($8 \to 5$ filtration observed, binomial distribution $C(6,k)$, validation on 8 historical cases) is the ultimate argument -- not the demonstration.

\textbf{Assumed status.} A1 is a \textbf{hermeneutic postulate}, not a theorem. It is coherent with the structure of the Merkabah and fruitful (it produces the $8 \to 5$ filtration), but it is not demonstrated. The word "founded" (Y.8) is too strong: A1 is \textbf{motivated}, not \textbf{founded}.

#### Y.3.2. Theorem T1 (combinatorial purity)

\textbf{Definition Y.2 (pure / mixed octahedron).} An octahedron is said to be \textbf{pure} if no pair of adjacent faces simultaneously bears the polarity $+$. It is said to be \textbf{mixed} (or frustrated) if at least one pair of adjacent faces simultaneously bears the polarity $+$.

\textbf{Theorem T1.} Under axiom A1, an octahedron whose 3 regions are coded by $(b_3, b_4, b_5)$ with adjacencies $(b_3, b_4)$ and $(b_4, b_5)$ is pure if and only if:

$$b_3 b_4 = 0 \quad \wedge \quad b_4 b_5 = 0$$

\textbf{Demonstration.}

- $(\Rightarrow)$ If the octahedron is pure, then by definition no adjacent pair is co-activated. In particular, $(b_3, b_4)$ and $(b_4, b_5)$ are not co-activated, therefore $b_3 b_4 = 0$ and $b_4 b_5 = 0$.
- $(\Leftarrow)$ If $b_3 b_4 = 0$ and $b_4 b_5 = 0$, then the two adjacent pairs are not co-activated. By convention Y.1, these are the only adjacent pairs. Therefore the octahedron is pure. QED

\textbf{Remark.} This theorem is a \textbf{well-formulated tautology}: it explicits the content of definition Y.2 given convention Y.1. Its value is pedagogical and structural, not demonstrative in the strong sense. The true physical hypothesis is A1.

#### Y.3.3. Theorem T2 (equivalence with R1--R3)

\textbf{Theorem T2.} The rules (R1), (R2), (R3) are equivalent to the purity condition $b_3 b_4 = 0 \wedge b_4 b_5 = 0$.

\textbf{Demonstration.}

- \textbf{(R1)} $b_3 + b_4 + b_5 \leq 2$. If $b_3 = b_4 = b_5 = 1$, then $b_3 b_4 = 1$ and $b_4 b_5 = 1$, which violates purity. Therefore purity implies (R1). Reciprocally, if (R1) is violated, then $b_3 = b_4 = b_5 = 1$, therefore purity is violated.
- \textbf{(R2)} $b_3 = 0 \Rightarrow b_4 + b_5 \leq 1$. If $b_3 = 0$ and $b_4 = b_5 = 1$, then $b_4 b_5 = 1$, which violates purity. Therefore purity implies (R2). Reciprocally, if (R2) is violated, then $b_4 b_5 = 1$, therefore purity is violated.
- \textbf{(R3)} $b_5 = 0 \Rightarrow b_3 + b_4 \leq 1$. If $b_5 = 0$ and $b_3 = b_4 = 1$, then $b_3 b_4 = 1$, which violates purity. Therefore purity implies (R3). Reciprocally, if (R3) is violated, then $b_3 b_4 = 1$, therefore purity is violated.

The three rules are therefore equivalent to purity. QED

---

#### Y.4.2. Geometric interpretation

The 3 frustrated configurations violate polar parsimony: \textbf{011} ($b_4 = b_5 = 1$, co-activation of the adjacent faces $F_4, F_5$); \textbf{110} ($b_3 = b_4 = 1$, co-activation of $F_3, F_4$); \textbf{111} (simultaneous co-activation of $(F_3, F_4)$ and $(F_4, F_5)$).

In each case, two $+$ tetrahedra find themselves attached along an edge, creating a local frustration incompatible with the global polar closure.

---

### Y.5. Link with Rowlands' nilpotency -- assumed hermeneutic circle

#### Y.5.1. Nilpotency as algebraic foundation

In the Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(6,0)$, Rowlands' nilpotency condition is written $(g \cdot x)^2 = 0$. This condition applies to an \textbf{ideal} generated by a primitive projector $\Pi$, and not to a raw vector. For Group B, the element associated with a configuration $(b_3, b_4, b_5)$ is:

$$X = \left( b_3 \, e_4 + b_4 \, e_5 + b_5 \, e_6 \right) \Pi$$

where $e_4, e_5, e_6$ are generators of $\mathrm{Cl}(6,0)$ and $\Pi$ a primitive projector.

#### Y.5.2. Calculation of $X^2$ and cancellation of bivectorial terms

Let us calculate $X^2$:

$$X^2 = \left( b_3 e_4 + b_4 e_5 + b_5 e_6 \right) \Pi \left( b_3 e_4 + b_4 e_5 + b_5 e_6 \right) \Pi$$

In the ideal, the projection relations impose $\Pi e_i \Pi = \Pi e_i$ for the relevant generators. The diagonal terms give $b_i^2 e_i^2 \Pi = b_i \Pi$ (because $e_i^2 = +1$). The crossed terms give bivectors $b_i b_j e_i e_j \Pi$.

\textbf{The nilpotency $X^2 = 0$ requires the simultaneous cancellation of the scalar part and of the bivectorial parts.}

- Scalar part: $b_3 + b_4 + b_5 = 0$, which is satisfied only by $b_3 = b_4 = b_5 = 0$. This condition is \textbf{too restrictive} and does not discriminate the 5 valid configurations.
- Bivectorial parts: the terms $b_3 b_4 \, e_4 e_5$ and $b_4 b_5 \, e_5 e_6$ must cancel.

#### Y.5.3. Postulated equivalence E1

\textbf{Equivalence E1 (nilpotency $\leftrightarrow$ polar parsimony).} The condition of cancellation of the bivectorial terms of $X^2$ in the Clifford ideal is equivalent to axiom A1 of polar parsimony.

\textbf{Justification.} In Rowlands' formalism, nilpotency requires not only the cancellation of the scalar part, but also that of the interaction components (bivectors) to guarantee polar closure. By projecting this condition onto Group B, the crossed terms involve the products $b_3 b_4$ (interaction between $F_3$ and $F_4$) and $b_4 b_5$ (interaction between $F_4$ and $F_5$). For the global state to be nilpotent -- that is, closed on itself without polar residue -- these interactions must cancel, which imposes $b_3 b_4 = 0$ and $b_4 b_5 = 0$.

\textbf{Status.} E1 is a \textbf{postulated equivalence}, not demonstrated in the strict sense. It is plausible and coherent with Rowlands' formalism, but its complete demonstration would require a detailed analysis of the Clifford ideal, which exceeds the framework of this appendix. \textbf{The hermeneutic circle A1 $\leftrightarrow$ E1 is explicitly assumed} (see Y.3.1).

#### Y.5.4. The geometric resolution of the symmetry breaking $8 \to 5$

In his work, Rowlands identifies a fundamental symmetry breaking reducing the 8 primitive units to 5 composite units, and underlines the importance of this structure for the genetic code:

> "Within the algebra of symmetry breaking there is the reduction from 8 to 5-fold symmetry which we can represent by packing 5 tetrahedra into a disk." [@Hill_Rowlands_2007, p. 541]

He even specifies:

> "Considering the original eight, the octahedron would serve as a good candidate for this analogy." [@Hill_Rowlands_2007, p. 541]

\textbf{Interpretation.} Rowlands speaks of \textbf{analogy} and of \textbf{candidate}, not of derivation. The present appendix proposes a \textbf{geometric resolution} of this intuition: the reduction from 8 to 5 is not a simple analogy, but a \textbf{topological necessity} dictated by A1 (polar parsimony). By forbidding the co-activation of polarities $+$ on adjacent faces, the structure of the octahedron filters the 8 mathematically possible configurations to retain only the 5 "pure" configurations.

This topological mechanism is the \textbf{candidate interface} between the Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(6,0)$ and the $64 \to 20$ filtration of the genetic code observed in the level 3 Merkabah.

---

### Y.6. Link with the genetic code -- programmatic conjecture

#### Y.6.1. The $64 \to 20$ filtration of the genetic code

Hill \& Rowlands [@Hill_Rowlands_2007, §7] show that the genetic code realises a $64 \to 20$ filtration:

> "The transcription and translation of the 64 codons of DNA into 20 amino acid building blocks of protein is analogous to the resolution of the 64 units of algebra into 20 in the fermionic nilpotent."

This filtration is \textbf{structurally analogous} to that of Group B.

#### Y.6.2. The topological neighbourhood rule

The document [@DeDominicis_2026_Tian_Dao_AI] gives the neighbourhood rule:

> "Two configurations are said to be neighbours if and only if the corresponding tetrahedra share an entire triangular face."

#### Y.6.3. Conjecture C1 (isomorphism)

\textbf{Conjecture C1.} The $8 \to 5$ filtration of Group B is isomorphic to the $64 \to 20$ filtration of the genetic code, in the sense that both rely on a rule of compatibility of adjacent faces.

\textbf{What is established.} The two filtrations exist: Group B: $8 \to 5$ (demonstrated under A1, T3); genetic code: $64 \to 20$ (observed, Hill \& Rowlands 2007).

\textbf{What is missing for a substantive conjecture.}

1. \textbf{Explicit bijection} between the 5 valid configurations and 5 classes of codons. No canonical bijection is known.
2. \textbf{Preservation of the neighbourhood structure}: the bijection must send adjacent faces to adjacent faces.
3. \textbf{Extension to the 64 codons and 20 amino acids}: the conjecture bears on $8 \to 5$, not on $64 \to 20$.

\textbf{Illustrative example -- and why it does not suffice.}

One can construct \textit{a} correspondence table between the 5 valid configurations and 5 classes of codons (for example: 000 $\leftrightarrow$ Phe, 001 $\leftrightarrow$ Leu, 010 $\leftrightarrow$ Ser, 100 $\leftrightarrow$ Tyr, 101 $\leftrightarrow$ Cys). But this table is \textbf{arbitrary}: nothing guarantees that it preserves the neighbourhood structure, nor that it extends to the 64 codons. It illustrates the \textit{possibility} of a bijection, not its \textit{canonical existence}.

\textbf{Assumed status.} C1 is a \textbf{programmatic conjecture}, not substantive. It indicates a direction of research (construct the explicit bijection), not a result.

#### Y.6.4. Comparative table

| Aspect | Genetic code | Group B |
|---|---|---|
| Input | 64 codons | 8 configurations |
| Output | 20 amino acids | 5 valid |
| Filtration | Neighbourhood rule | Purity rule (A1) |
| Structure | Octahedra + tetrahedra | Octahedra |
| Rule | Compatibility of faces | $b_3 b_4 = 0$, $b_4 b_5 = 0$ |
| Status | Observed | Demonstrated under A1 |

### Y.7. Synthesis

#### Y.7.1. The logic of octahedra

The frustration of configurations 011, 110, 111 is explained by the \textbf{structure of the octahedra} of the Merkabah:

1. The 8 configurations of Group B correspond to the 8 octahedra.
2. The 3 bits $(b_3, b_4, b_5)$ code the polarity of three faces adjacent along a meridian (convention Y.1).
3. Axiom A1 (polar parsimony) forbids the co-activation of two adjacent faces in polarity $+$.
4. Theorem T1 deduces from it the purity rule $b_3 b_4 = 0$ and $b_4 b_5 = 0$.
5. Theorem T2 shows the equivalence with (R1), (R2), (R3).
6. Theorem T3 (filtration $8 \to 5$) enumerates the 5 valid configurations.

#### Y.7.2. Link with nilpotency

The equivalence E1 postulates that the nilpotency condition $(g \cdot x)^2 = 0$, projected onto the Clifford ideal of Group B, is equivalent to axiom A1. Nilpotency is the \textbf{algebraic foundation}; polar parsimony is the \textbf{topological manifestation}. The hermeneutic circle A1 $\leftrightarrow$ E1 is explicitly assumed (Y.3.1).

#### Y.7.3. Link with the genetic code

Conjecture C1 postulates that the $64 \to 20$ filtration of the genetic code is isomorphic to the $8 \to 5$ filtration of Group B. The topological neighbourhood rule is the analogue of the purity rule. The complete demonstration remains to be made.

### Y.8. Conclusion

This appendix has \textbf{motivated} the frustration of configurations 011, 110, 111 of Group B on the structure of the octahedra of the Merkabah, by rigorously distinguishing:

- a \textbf{physical axiom A1} (polar parsimony), postulated and motivated by the rarity of positive tetrahedra;
- a \textbf{combinatorial theorems T1--T3}, demonstrated under A1, which produce the $8 \to 5$ filtration;
- a \textbf{postulated equivalence E1} between Rowlands' nilpotency and A1;
- a \textbf{conjecture C1} of isomorphism with the $64 \to 20$ filtration of the genetic code.

\textbf{What this appendix establishes.} Theorems T1--T3 are demonstrated. The $8 \to 5$ filtration is a certain combinatorial result, subject to accepting A1.

\textbf{What this appendix does not establish.} A1 is not demonstrated; it is motivated. E1 is not demonstrated; it is postulated. C1 is not demonstrated; it is conjectured.

\textbf{Global status.} Appendix Y is \textbf{rigorous in its structuring} (distinction A1 / T1--T3 / E1 / C1) but \textbf{non-demonstrative in its foundation} (A1 is a postulate). It fills the gap of the main text (rule R1--R3 was stated without justification) while remaining honest about the epistemic status of each statement. The two open research programmes -- demonstration of E1 and explicit construction of the bijection C1 -- are clearly identified.

---

### Y.9. Technical notes

#### Y.9.1. On the choice of convention Y.1

Convention Y.1 (three faces along a meridian, two adjacent pairs, one non-adjacent pair) is motivated by the necessity of producing exactly the $8 \to 5$ filtration. An alternative choice (three adjacent pairs, for example three faces around a vertex) would produce the $8 \to 4$ filtration:

| Code | Three adjacent pairs? |
|---|---|
| 000 | ✓ |
| 001 | ✓ |
| 010 | ✓ |
| 011 | ✗ |
| 100 | ✓ |
| 101 | ✗ |
| 110 | ✗ |
| 111 | ✗ |

Only 000, 001, 010, 100 would survive, i.e., 4 configurations. The $8 \to 5$ filtration of the main text therefore imposes convention Y.1 (only two adjacent pairs).

#### Y.9.2. On the status of equivalence E1

Equivalence E1 is \textbf{plausible} but not demonstrated. Its complete demonstration would require: (1) explicitly constructing the Clifford ideal generated by the projector $\Pi$; (2) calculating $X^2$ in this ideal, taking into account the projection relations; (3) showing that the cancellation of the bivectorial terms is equivalent to $b_3 b_4 = 0$ and $b_4 b_5 = 0$. This demonstration is a \textbf{research programme} in its own right.

#### Y.9.3. On conjecture C1

Conjecture C1 is \textbf{heuristic}. Its demonstration would require: (1) identifying the octahedral structure in the genetic code (do the 64 codons distribute themselves into 8 groups of 8?); (2) constructing an explicit bijection between the 5 valid configurations and 5 classes of codons; (3) verifying the preservation of the neighbourhood structure. These three steps are open.

\textbf{End of Appendix Y.}

---

## Appendix Z -- Topological derivation of the borromean cohesion of the 400 pairs of attractors

### Z.0. Object and positioning

#### Z.0.1. Articulation with Appendices T and X

Appendix X has established the \textbf{combinatorial classification} of the 400 pairs of joint attractors. Appendix T has clarified the distinction between the \textbf{base potential} $\mathcal{B}_0$ (defined in T.2.3) and the \textbf{general borromean cohesion} $\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}}$ (defined in T.3.5). The present appendix (Z) provides the \textbf{topological derivation} of the general formula and the \textbf{numbered catalogue} of the 400 values of $\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}}$.

> \textbf{Reading note.} The base potential $\mathcal{B}_0$ (defined in T.2.3) is a \textit{term} of the general formula. The numerical values presented in this appendix (§Z.5--Z.10) are the final values of $\mathcal{B}_{\text{joint}}$, obtained after application of the general formula integrating the topological friction and the hierarchical modulation. The general formula is defined \textbf{once only} in T.3.5; the present appendix applies it, it does not redefine it.

#### Z.0.2. The two levels of analysis

Appendix Z articulates two levels of analysis:

| Level | Object | Method | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Topological | The 20 attractors and their relations | Strict hierarchical graph (60 edges) | Structural classification |
| Spectral | The signatures $\varepsilon^* \in \{-1,0,1\}^{15}$ | Projection $\Pi$ via $P_{48 \times 15}$ | Validation and derivation |

The fundamental observation is that these two levels are orthogonal: the Spearman correlation between topological distances and spectral distances is null ($\rho = 0.023$, $p = 0.656$). They do not describe the same reality. The topological level describes the structure of the relations between attractors, while the spectral level describes the internal stability of each attractor. The classification of the 400 pairs is therefore done at the topological level. The spectral level serves to validate and to derive the cohesion formula.

\subsection*{Z.0.5. Synthesis: the three levels of objects and the place of Appendix Z}

Before entering into the technical detail of the topological derivation, it is useful to recall the \textbf{three-level hierarchy} which structures the whole model, and to specify \emph{where} Appendix Z is situated in this hierarchy. This clarification avoids a frequent confusion: that which consists in believing that the pairs of attractors (level C) are geo-economic states (level A).

\paragraph{The three levels.}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{The three levels of objects of the $\mathrm{Cl}(6,6)$ model}
\label{tab:Z05_trois_niveaux}
\small
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{|>{\centering\arraybackslash}p{1.2cm}|>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.6cm}|>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.4cm}|>{\centering\arraybackslash}p{1.4cm}|>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X|}
\hline
\textbf{Level} & \textbf{Object} & \textbf{Combination} & \textbf{Number} & \textbf{Role} \\
\hline
\textbf{A} & Geo-economic state & Pair of pentads $X_a \otimes Y_b$ ($X \in \{P,N\}$, $Y \in \{G,H\}$) & 144 & Position in the grid (conjunction of two configurations) \\
\hline
\textbf{B} & Attractor & Triplet of pentads $\{X_i, Y_j, Z_k\}$ & 40 (20 eco + 20 geo) & Configuration label (coding of a 3-bit binary configuration) \\
\hline
\textbf{C} & Pair of attractors & Pair of attractors $(A_{\text{eco}}, A_{\text{geo}})$ & 400 & Relation between two salient configurations \\
\hline
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

\paragraph{The chain of dependence.}

These three levels do not nest by inclusion: they are of \textbf{different natures}. The correct relation between them is a \textbf{projection chain}:

$$
\underbrace{\text{Attractor (level B)}}_{\text{triplet}}
\;\xrightarrow{\ \text{encodes}\ }\;
\underbrace{\text{Binary configuration}}_{\text{3 bits}}
\;\xrightarrow{\ \text{indexes}\ }\;
\underbrace{\text{Class of states (level A)}}_{\text{positions}}.
$$

An attractor encodes a configuration (for example \texttt{000/010}); this configuration indexes the class of states which share it. An attractor thus "marks" a \textbf{class of states}, not an isolated state.

Level C is added downstream: a pair puts in relation \textbf{two triplets}, therefore indirectly \textbf{two classes of states}. The 400 pairs are the relations between salient configurations, and not objects of level A or B.

\paragraph{Where Appendix Z operates.}

Each appendix operates at a specific level, and it is important not to confuse them:

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{The appendices and their level of operation}
\label{tab:Z05_annexes_niveaux}
\small
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{|>{\centering\arraybackslash}p{1.4cm}|>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X|>{\centering\arraybackslash}p{1.6cm}|}
\hline
\textbf{Appendix} & \textbf{Object} & \textbf{Level} \\
\hline
\textbf{C} & The 144 states (positions); the 40 attractors (labels); the distinction between the two & A and B \\
\hline
\textbf{T} & Interpretation of remarkable pairs (Stasis, bubble, optimum) and empirical validation & C \\
\hline
\textbf{X} & \emph{Combinatorial} classification of the 400 pairs (polarities, forbidden states) & C \\
\hline
\textbf{Z} (present) & \emph{Topological} derivation of the 400 pairs (graph, formula, numbered catalogue) & C \\
\hline
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

Appendix Z therefore operates at \textbf{level C}: it qualifies the 400 pairs of attractors by their borromean cohesion, their fragility, and their viability. It does \textbf{not} describe the 144 states (level A, which belong to Appendix C) nor the 40 isolated attractors (level B, which belong to Appendix A and Appendix N).

\paragraph{Three precisions to avoid confusions.}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A pair is not a state.} The pair $(S_{\text{eco}}, S_{\text{geo}})$ (economic Stasis × territorial Stasis) is not the state $N_5 \otimes H_5$ (ID 137). The state $N_5 \otimes H_5$ is a \emph{position}; the pair $(S_{\text{eco}}, S_{\text{geo}})$ is a \emph{configuration label} which projects onto this position (and onto others).
\item \textbf{The 400 pairs do not replace the 144 states.} They \emph{overarch} them: each state is described by 25 accessible pairs (pentad constraint), and the catalogue Z.7.7 qualifies these 25 pairs. Table C.5 (144 states with historical examples) and the catalogue Z.7.7 (400 pairs with numerical values) are \textbf{complementary}, not redundant nor contradictory.
\item \textbf{The historical examples of C.5 illustrate the states, not the pairs.} An example like "Shenzhen SEZ (1980--2000)" for the state $P_4 \otimes G_3$ illustrates a \emph{conjunction} of two configurations (an export regime deploying itself on a territory with dense mesh). It does not illustrate a pair of attractors. The remarkable pairs are historically illustrated in Appendix T, §T.5 (8 calibrated cases).
\end{enumerate}

The three levels are complementary and project onto each other, without ever being confused.

\subsection*{Z.0.6. Correspondence table: one state → its 25 accessible pairs}

\paragraph{Principle.}

Each state $E_{k,j} = X_k \otimes Y_j$ (level A) is described by \textbf{25 pairs} of attractors (level C), obtained by Cartesian product of the 5 economic attractors containing $X_k$ and the 5 geographic attractors containing $Y_j$. This section provides the correspondence table which allows passing from a state to its 25 pairs.

\paragraph{Why 25?}

Each pentad $X_k$ belongs to exactly \textbf{5 triplets} (out of the 20 economic attractors); each pentad $Y_j$ belongs to exactly \textbf{5 triplets} (out of the 20 geographic attractors). Therefore the state $X_k \otimes Y_j$ is described by $5 \times 5 = 25$ pairs. This property is verified on tables \ref{tab:Z06_pentades_eco} and \ref{tab:Z06_pentades_geo}.

### Z.1. The $64 \to 15$ bits correspondence: reminder and extraction

#### Z.1.1. The operator $\Pi$ and the canonical section $\sigma$

The projection operator $\Pi : \mathcal{S} \to \mathcal{C}_{64}$ transforms the ternary signatures $\varepsilon \in \{-1,0,1\}^{15}$ into binary configurations of 6 bits, elements of $\mathrm{Cl}(6,0)$. It decomposes into three steps:

$$\Pi = \Phi_{\text{Merkabah}} \circ \Phi_{\text{Clifford}} \circ \Phi_{\beta}$$

The step $\Phi_\beta$ performs the spectral projection $\Phi_\beta(\varepsilon) = P_{48 \times 15} \cdot \varepsilon = \mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{R}^{48}$, where $P_{48 \times 15} = V_{48}^T \cdot V_{15}$ is the projection matrix. The step $\Phi_{\text{Clifford}}$ selects the 6 dominant components of $\mathbf{r}$ and discretises them into binary bits. The step $\Phi_{\text{Merkabah}}$ is the identity: the binary configuration is already in 6-bit format.

The canonical section $\sigma$ associates to each configuration $c \in \mathcal{C}_{64}$ a unique signature $\varepsilon^*(c)$ which maximises $\Delta(\varepsilon) = \sum_k \varepsilon_k \beta_k$ among all the admissible signatures projecting onto $c$.

#### Z.1.2. The matrix $E$ (64 × 15) and its structural constraints

From the 64 admissible signatures, one constructs the matrix $E \in \{-1,0,1\}^{64 \times 15}$. Its properties are: rank 14 (instead of 15), infinite conditioning, constant columns $\varepsilon_{14} = \varepsilon_{15} = -1$, effective space of 13 dimensions. The two largest constants $\beta_{14} = 4.724740$ and $\beta_{15} = 7.407963$ are always subtracted. The nilpotency condition $\Delta > 0$ imposes that the other components compensate this subtraction.

#### Z.1.3. The 64 admissible signatures: binomial distribution $C(6,k)$

The exhaustive exploration of the $3^{15} = 14\,348\,907$ ternary signatures reveals that only 64 signatures satisfy the nilpotency condition $\Delta > 0$ and produce unique binary configurations. The distribution by grade $k$ follows exactly the binomial law $C(6,k)$:

| Grade $k$ | Observed | Expected $C(6,k)$ | Deviation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 1 | 6 | 6 | 0 |
| 2 | 15 | 15 | 0 |
| 3 | 20 | 20 | 0 |
| 4 | 15 | 15 | 0 |
| 5 | 6 | 6 | 0 |
| 6 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| Total | 64 | 64 | 0 |

This perfect binomial distribution is the combinatorial signature of $\mathrm{Cl}(6,0)$.

The 20 economic attractors and the 20 geographic attractors are identified by their binary configurations according to the Merkabah mapping. For each attractor, the signature $\varepsilon^*$ is extracted by associating its binary configuration to the corresponding canonical signature in the 64 admissible signatures.

#### Z.1.6. Status of the 15 indices $I_{15}$ -- epistemic clarification

The 15 indices $I_{15} = \{3, 9, 10, 11, 15, 21, 24, 25, 29, 31, 33, 41, 48, 58, 72\}$ are the indices of the eigenvalues of $G_{72}$ whose square roots coincide with the 15 constants $\beta_k$.

\textbf{What we know.} The 15 indices are associated with the 15 constants $\beta_k$ of the lattice $\Lambda_{72}$ (numerical values in Z.1.2 of Chapter 15). The distribution of admissible signatures follows exactly the binomial law $C(6,k)$ (Z.1.3), which suggests that the 15 indices are \textbf{structured by the geometry of $\mathrm{Cl}(6,0)$}.

\textbf{What we do not know.} The \textit{derived} origin of the 15 indices from the structure of $\Lambda_{72}$ is not established. Four concurrent hypotheses are open:

1. \textbf{Hypothesis $SL_2(25) \times PSL_2(7):2$}: the 15 indices form a union of orbits under a stabilising subgroup of the automorphism group of $\Lambda_{72}$.
2. \textbf{Quebbemann hypothesis}: the 15 indices correspond to arithmetic properties of the polarisation $(M,N)$ in the construction $\Lambda_{72} = \Lambda(\Lambda_{24}, M, N, 3)$.
3. \textbf{Clifford centroids hypothesis}: the 15 indices correspond to the quadratic discriminants of a canonical orthogonal decomposition of $\Lambda_{72}$.
4. \textbf{Geometric Algebra hypothesis}: the 15 indices are the spectral invariants $\mathcal{I}(B_k)$ of the 15 bivectors of $\mathrm{Cl}(6,0)$, calculated via the projection matrix $P_{48 \times 15}$.

\textbf{Assumed status.} In the current state, the 15 indices are treated as an \textbf{operational black box}: they work (the binomial distribution and the predictions of Z.9 are validated), but their origin is not demonstrated. This black box is explicitly signalled as a research programme (Z.11.2, priority 1). The \textbf{bijection between the 15 bivectors of $\mathrm{Cl}(6,0)$ and the 15 constants $\beta_k$ is an arbitrary convention} (there exist $15! \approx 1.3 \times 10^{12}$ possible permutations), not a discovery.

### Z.2. The topological structure of the level 3 Merkabah

#### Z.2.1. Reminder: the Merkabah as star tetrahedron

According to Hill and Rowlands (2008), the level 3 Merkabah is a star tetrahedron, that is to say two level 3 tetrahedra interpenetrated. Its structure is: 8 internal octahedra (unstable zones, excluded from the filtration), 20 external tetrahedra (stable attractors), 64 triangular faces (configurations of $\mathrm{Cl}(6,0)$), 5 groups of 4 tetrahedra (5-fold symmetry).

The $64 \to 20$ filtration is defined by the neighbourhood rule: two configurations are in the same class if their tetrahedra share an entire triangular face.

#### Z.2.2. The 8 internal octahedra and the 20 external tetrahedra

The 8 internal octahedra each have 8 triangular faces, which gives 64 faces, corresponding to the 64 configurations. The 20 external tetrahedra are the 20 stable attractors. The distribution of polarities is: 3P (3: A, B, C), 2P+1N (5: D, E, F, G, H), 1P+2N (11: I, J, K, L, M, N, O, P, Q, R, S), 3N (1: T).

#### Z.2.3. The $64 \to 20$ filtration

The $64 \to 20$ filtration is a partition of the space of 64 configurations into 20 equivalence classes. Each class is an attractor in the sense of a topologically closed basin. The mechanism is the following: two configurations are in the same class if their tetrahedra share an entire triangular face. The partition is rigid under the automorphism group of the double tetrahedron.

#### Z.2.4. The hierarchy of the 20 attractors

The 20 attractors are organised into 7 hierarchical levels:

| Level | Attractors | Number | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | A | 1 | Reference pole |
| 1 | B, C, D, E | 4 | Cardinal faces |
| 2 | F, G, H, I | 4 | Edges |
| 3 | J, K, L, M | 4 | Vertices |
| 4 | N, O, P | 3 | Diagonals |
| 5 | Q, R, S | 3 | Intersections |
| 6 | T | 1 | Internal core |
| Total | | 20 | |

This hierarchy is determined by the geometric position of the tetrahedra in the Merkabah, as documented in the file `graphe_dual_pentades_attracteurs.csv`.

#### Z.2.5. The 5-fold symmetry and the 4 communities

The level 3 Merkabah possesses a pentagonal symmetry (5-fold), broken from the 8-fold symmetry of the Clifford algebra. This symmetry manifests itself in the 5 groups of 4 tetrahedra, in the 12 pentagonal faces of the dual dodecahedron, and in the 4 emergent communities of the hierarchical graph:

| Community | Vertices | Levels |
|---|---|---|
| C1 | C, D, K, M, Q | Mixed |
| C2 | B, F, J, L, P | Mixed |
| C3 | E, H, N, R, T | Mixed |
| C4 | A, G, I, O, S | Mixed |

Each community contains 5 attractors, reflecting the 5-fold symmetry.

### Z.4. Topological analysis of the hierarchical graph

#### Z.4.1. Topological distances between the 20 attractors

The matrix of topological distances ($20 \times 20$) is calculated by `nx.shortest_path_length`. The statistics are: distance min 1, distance max 6, mean distance 2.18, median distance 2.00. The distribution of distances shows that the majority of pairs are at distance 2 or 3, with some pairs at distance 1 (the edges) and some pairs at distance 5 or 6 (the topological opposites).

The diagonals (N, O, P) have the maximal betweenness (0.1108). They are the obligatory passage points between the upper and lower levels.

\textbf{Betweenness} translates \textbf{betweenness}: frequency at which an attractor finds itself on the shortest paths between two others. To be distinguished from \emph{closeness} (\emph{closeness}).}

#### Z.4.3. The diagonals as tipping points

The attractors N, O, P (level 4) are the tipping points of the system. They are connected to the vertices (J, K, L, M) and to the intersections (Q, R, S). Any transition between the high regimes (levels 0-3) and the low regimes (levels 5-6) must pass through them. Their high betweenness confirms their critical role. In economic terms, the diagonals are bifurcation points in the system. Any transition policy must target them in priority.

#### Z.4.4. Emergent communities

The graph partitions itself into 2 communities detected by `greedy_modularity_communities`: Community 1 (A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, K, M; levels 0-2 + K, M) and Community 2 (J, L, N, O, P, Q, R, S, T; levels 3-6 + J, L). The partition is asymmetrical (11 vs 9) and does not strictly follow the levels. It is an emergent structure which reflects the privileged connections between certain attractors.

#### Z.4.5. Structural interpretation

|---|---|
| 7 hierarchical levels | Nested structure of the Merkabah |
| Varied degrees (3 to 11) | Distinct topological roles |
| Maximal betweenness for N, O, P | Tipping points |
| 2 asymmetrical communities | Emergent structure |

The hierarchical graph captures the real topological structure of the Merkabah, contrary to the regular dodecahedron which is too symmetrical.
